speakeroldname: Mr. Francois Gerin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE AND CANADA EVIDENCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to address the substance of Bill C-15, but first of all, I would like to acknowledge the important work done by members of the Legislative Committee.
I was also very impressed by the statements of the witnesses. Their testimony proved to be very useful in considering a Bill that is so important for Canada's children and young people. The Bill was well received by those who regularly care for children who have been victims of sexual assault, although proposals were made to amend some of the provisions of the Bill.
Indeed, we agreed to introduce some major amendments to improve certain aspects so that the Bill will more effectively protect children and young people against sexual assault. Furthermore, this Bill seeks to reinforce the rights of victims by facilitating access to the judicial system.
Another purpose of this Bill is to identify offenders and give them a chance to receive the support and treatment they need. On the whole, the Bill's structure is much the same as it was when the House decided to refer it to a legislative committee.
Basically, the Bill contains three important measures. First of all, in order to provide additional protection against sexual abuse, it creates three new offences relating to the sexual abuse of children and young people. Second, the Bill abolishes certain offences under the Criminal Code that have become obsolete and amends provisions relating to other offences to make the Criminal Code more effective and more attuned to today's society. Third, the Bill provides for ways to enable children to testify.
The Bill therefore contains three new offences. To protect children under fourteen years of age, it creates the offence of
sexual interference. Every person who, for sexual purposes, touches a child under fourteen years of age is liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding ten years.
Children under fourteen years of age are also protected by a new offence which consists in inviting a child of that age to engage in sexual touching of others. This offence would also carry a maximum prison term of ten years.
The third new offence is aimed at protecting young people under eighteen years of age from sexual exploitation by any person who is in a situation of trust or authority towards these young people. In very serious cases, the offence would carry a maximum prison term of five years. Furthermore, each of these offences may be punishable on summary conviction.
Since for each offence, the legislation emphasizes the terms "for sexual purposes", the Crown will have to prove that those purposes are one of the essential components of the crime. In this way, parents, teachers and all persons involved in caring for children will be protected against frivolous charges.
Anyone who takes care of children knows that they have to be hugged and shown love and affection. The usual way we express love and affection, by touching the child in whatever way, is of course not what is meant by these new provisions.
Only the kind of contact or touching or invitation to touching that is aimed at awakening sexual desire or obtaining sexual satisfaction is covered by these offences. The Badgley Committee found that many sexual assaults against children and adolescents in Canada involve such touching. Liability may be attributed for each of these offences, even if there is an element of consent, or at least of non-opposition on the part of the victim. Of course, if there is no such consent to touching, the incident obviously constitutes a sexual assault. However, even if such consent exists, it cannot be used as a defence to a charge, except in a very few cases. It is necessary to provide for such an exception so as not to make criminal acts out of the normal sexual discovery activities of young people.
Under the Bill, if the accused is not in a position of trust or authority towards a child twelve years of age or more but under the age of sixteen and if he is not two years older than the complainant, consent can be used as a defence. I underline the fact that consent can be used as a defence in such cases. In fact, the Badgley Committee and the evidence given before the legislative committee both point out that young people who indulge in sexual touching with younger children can in fact be exploiting them.
The second major initiative contained in this Bill consists in amending existing sexual offences and eliminating some others. There is no need to explain why some outdated offences have been eliminated, such as those which deal with the seduction of young women or of female passengers by the crew of a ship. Such offences no longer lead to a charge. They have no place in a modern Criminal Code.
Other offences have been amended to reflect the evolution of our society and the changes required by the new provisions
June 23, 1987

contained in the Bill. These changes include the addition of two new offences which also, aim at protecting children and adolescents. The first concerns a person who, in any place, for a sexual purpose, exposes his or her genital organs to a person under the age of fourteen. Such indecent exposure was already covered by the Criminal Code if committed in public. However, if committed in private, there had to be in addition an intent to insult or offend. These provisions were found to be inadequate in cases where people showed their genital organs to children for a sexual purpose. The new provision therefore makes this an offense punishable on summary conviction.
Once more, I emphasize the fact that such exposure must be for a sexual purpose. This means that the simple fact of going around the house without any clothes on in the presence of children, for instance, will not constitute an offence.
The second offence concerns the customers of young prostitutes. From now on, requesting the sexual services of a person under the age of eighteen will constitute an offence.
According to many comments, the problem of juvenile prostitution is getting increasingly serious. These young people must be protected against the consequences of such activities. The Badgley Committee recommended that, as a last resort, prostitution by young persons constitute an indictable offence, but such a solution does not seem acceptable. It would be better to target the customers who use young people for sexual services. Consequently, those who request the sexual services of prostitutes under the age of eighteen will be liable to five years in prison in the most serious cases. In addition, to ensure that those who live on the avails of prostitution of young people are not simply soliciting for the prostitutes, the penalty for living on the avails of juvenile prostitution is being increased to fourteen years of imprisonment.
Existing provisions which deal with the evidence given by children reflect outdated attitudes as concerns the reliability of such evidence. While Common Law rules originally provided that anyone could be a witness for the Crown, women and children were gradually judged to be less than reliable witnesses, especially when giving evidence about sexual assaults of which they had been the victims. A major detail of the evidence given by women and children had to be corroborated by a piece of compromising evidence against the accused. Because of the very nature of these offences, however, it was impossible in many cases to find corroborating evidence. This injustice against women was corrected in 1976, and Bill C-127, which came into effect in 1983, clarified the applicable provisions. We are now attempting to repair the injustice done to children who have witnessed criminal acts.
There is increasing, convincing evidence that children who have to report on facts they have experienced are truthful witnesses. The injustice in denying child victims of criminal acts the right to explain the facts to the court has been recognized by the Badgley Committee and the Fraser Committee. Both committees recommended repealing the rule requiring corroboration.
Criminal Code
The corroboration rule prevented a child from obtaining justice. Moreover, the rules on child evidence often prevented children from explaining to the court what they had experienced. Even though a child was called to the witness box, seeing his alleged aggressor often disconcerted him to the point where he could not give coherent evidence.
The Bill would allow children to more easily report on acts they have been victims of, in keeping with the accused's rights. It would also allow a larger number of children to give evidence. Any child who could state the facts and promise to tell the truth could give evidence. Such evidence would be heard by a judge or jury, who would determine its credibility. So that he could give a full and truthful statement of the facts on which the charges are based, a provision could be used by the court to allow the child to testify without seeing the accused.
That goal could be reached by putting a screen in the courtroom or by having the child in another room. In the latter case, the other parties involved should be given an opportunity to attend the testimony on closed circuit television. The child no longer would be put under the obligation of repeating the recital of facts because the Bill includes a provision under which a videotape could be made within a reasonable period after the alleged offence has been commited.
The effect of that proposal could be to avoid the child having to repeat the same evidence, often a number of times. It would also enable the child to make in his own words a recent report of the facts while they are still fresh in his or her memory.
So that such a videotape could be allowed in evidence, the child would of course have to confirm the contents when testifying before the courts. The child could then be cross-examined, which cross-examination would clearly have to be led in light of the child's age and ability to understand if the court were to be able to take it into account.
Mr. Speaker, I only referred to the most significant aspects of the Bill, which is aimed at protecting children and youth against sexual aggressions by creating new offences, and to make it easier for children to access the criminal justice system.
On the other hand, the proposals are based on the principle that the rights of the accused also have to be respected. When such sweeping changes are being introduced into an area of the law that is of such tremendous importance, the impact of course has to be carefully reviewed. Steps have therefore been taken for such a review to be initiated immediately and for a report to be submitted to a committee four years from now. A complete review could then be made of the impact of the implementation of those legislative proprosals.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this important debate and to echo the comments which have been made by the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) who certainly played an important and constructive role in the work of the legislative committee on Bill C-15.
Criminal Code
I have participated as the justice critic for my Party in many legislative committees and in many sittings of the justice committee on legislation. I can say without any hesitation whatsoever that I felt the work done in this committee, chaired I might add by Your Honour, was really outstanding.
The committee looked at a piece of legislation dealing with a very important, sensitive, and complex question. We heard from many witnesses from across Canada, such as groups representing the Child Welfare Community and the Canadian Council on Children and Youth, which had conducted its own extensive hearings and consultations in respect of the legislation. Many witnesses voiced their concerns about the legislation.
In a truly non-partisan spirit the legislative committee, after having heard from these witnesses, proposed some very significant amendments to the legislation. I see the Parliamentary Secretary in the House who spoke earlier on the debate representing the Minister. I can say that there were times when perhaps the Parliamentary Secretary was not entirely in agreement, as Your Honour will recall, with the spirit of some amendments proposed by members of the committee. Nevertheless, the committee as a whole, in a non-partisan approach, in fact made some very major and important improvements to the piece of legislation. I should like to touch upon some of the areas in which I believe the Bill has been significantly improved.
Before doing so, however, I should like to indicate my concern that while we are establishing a legislative framework today, it is an important and essential first step, but it is certainly not enough. We heard from a number of witnesses in the committee about the critical shortage of resources, both at the federal and provincial level, to deal with the concerns of the community, to deal with the sexual abuse of children.
It is one thing to establish a framework for prosecution of these offences, but it is quite another thing for us as a society, having done so, not to recognize that we are terribly underfunding programs to prevent child abuse, programs to deal with and to assist children to recover from the trauma of abuse, and programs to deal with those who offend.
Another area in which we received representations as a committee was in respect of the adult survivors of child abuse. This is an area in which further legislative action is clearly necessary. We must take steps to ensure that those adults who still bear the scars of abuse as children after, in some cases, many years must be in a position to come forward to tell their stories. There must be resources to ensure that they receive the kind of support they so desperately need.
I hope the Government will recognize that we have unfinished business here. Yes, we have taken important steps in respect of children who have been abused, and I welcome those steps. However, we must go further and deal with the very serious concerns which have been raised by adult survivors of abuse.

June 23, 1987
Criminal Code
It is clear that in too many parts of Canada, including my own Province of British Columbia, Governments pay lip service to the importance of resources for dealing with abused children. They quite properly call for effective enforcement mechanisms, but those same Governments fail miserably when it comes to providing support for children in our communities.
In this regard I should like to quote from a report of the National Council of Welfare entitled "Poor Kids". In part it reads:
Canadians like to believe that ours is a society in which all children are born with equal chances to rise as far as their abilities will carry them. Though they begin their lives in very disparate circumstances, we comfort ourselves with the belief that success is as attainable for the child of humblest origins as for the most affluent. The facts, however, are otherwise.
To be born poor in Canada does not make it a certainty that you will live poor and die poor-but it makes it very likely... The tax system and the income security system together determine the patterns of income redistribution in this country. The changes that are made in these systems as a result of the present federal provincial review-
And I might add the tax reform proposals:
-will affect the lives of every one of Canada's poor kids. New programs that
are adequate to raise Canada's poverty families out of poverty will transform
the futures of these poor kids. Inadequate programs will leave them facing the
grim prospects that mark the landscape of their lives today.
It is essential that we as a society pay far more attention in terms of resources for these children. They do not have a vote. They cannot speak in the House. Surely it is incumbent upon each and every Member of the House to recognize our obligations to the children of the country.
I should like to make another point before turning to some of the changes made in the legislative committee. The Government announced over a year ago that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) would shortly be announcing the appointment of a special adviser on child sexual abuse to co-ordinate activities at the federal level. The Badgley Commission recommended strongly that there must be a high level co-ordinator-indeed, Badgley recommended a co-ordinator attached to the Prime Minister's Office-to coordinate government activities at the federal level in the area of child abuse. The Minister of National Health and Welfare said that the special adviser would receive advice from a small committee of regional advisers who would bring forward ideas from different parts of the country and so on.
That commitment was made on January 10 of last year, over a year ago, and we are still waiting for the Government to live up to the promise it made to appoint that special adviser to take the kind of co-ordinating action so desperately needed across Canada.
The legislation before the House, Bill C-15, before the House was significantly improved by the work of the legislative committee that studied it. I would like to touch on two or three of the areas that I believe major changes were made to improve the Bill.
Perhaps the most important element of the legislation is the extent to which children are able to tell their stories in court and relate to the court in a manner in an and environment which is not threatening to them the experience they went through. The current provisions of the Criminal Code deny them that right. As the Canadian Council on Children and Youth stated, the fundamental and important element of the Bill is the degree to which victims of child sexual abuse have the opportunity to tell their stories in court. The original proposals did not clearly facilitate children telling their stories in court.
I am very pleased, Mr. Speaker, that the committee made important changes in this area of the legislation. Now, instead of there being a test of sufficient intelligence, which were the words used in the Bill, the sole test will be the ability of that child to communicate his or her story to the court. If necessary, the courts may want to use devices to assist children, anatomically correct dolls, for example. The courts may wish to use art work. The committee heard from a psychotherapist who demonstrated how children can tell their stories through art. That may be another avenue of approach.
Another important change made to the legislation was the change with respect to the actual giving of evidence. In the Bill as presented to the House there was provision for the accused to be removed from the courtroom. There was strong criticism of that and the committee came up with a compromise. We recognized that a child or a young witness can be intimidated by the presence of the person who is alleged to have abused them. We said we would not remove the accused from the courtroom, but we would allow for arrangements to be made for children to give their evidence in a manner in which they do not have to directly confront the accused. That compromise was important, and one which I am pleased the committee adopted.
The provisions with respect to the substantive offences, namely, the provisions with respect to the offences created for the sexual abuse of children were also significantly changed. What the committee had to wrestle with was, on the one hand, a clear concern that young children should be in any way exploited because of their age and exploited in a sexual way. On the other hand, we had to recognize the reality that teenagers do engage in sexual activity and do indeed engage in sexual exploration. The Bill as it was drafted did not recognize that reality.
The committee said that where teenagers are engaged in consensual activity, and there is an age difference of less than two years, that behaviour will not be the subject of criminal sanction. Again, I believe that was an important change to the legislation.
There does remain a weakness with respect to one element of the legislation, namely, the failure of the legislative committee to respond to virtually every witness who appeared before the committee, whether it be the Canadian Council on Children and Youth, the Canadian Psychological Association,
June 23, 1987

the Teachers Federation or the Attorney General of the Conservative Province of Saskatchewan, who called upon the Government to establish a uniform age of consent for all sexual activity. That recommendation was made some time ago by the special committee on equality rights, recognizing that the current provisions of the Criminal Code and, indeed, this Bill as it has been reported, does discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation.
As well, and perhaps just as serious, is the fact that the Bill would subject teenagers to lengthy terms of imprisonment for engaging in consensual sexual activity, which is not the subject of criminal sanction elsewhere. It is regrettable that the legislative committee refused to recognize the concerns raised in this area by virtually every witness who appeared before the committee, and to move forward on amendments in this area of the legislation as well.
Finally, I am pleased to note that one of the amendments adopted was a provision building in a review mechanism. I believe it was the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) who proposed this amendment. It is one that we welcomed and supported. We are embarked in major changes in this area of the law. There is no question about that. To the extent that this review process is built into the Bill, it is essential that the Department of Justice carefully monitor the implementation of this legislation in order that we as parliamentarians may be in a position to conduct the review properly at the time it comes, some three or four years from now.
It is clear, beyond doubt, that we have significantly improved the law in Canada with respect to children who have been victims of sexual abuse. It is vitally important that we now turn our attention to the scandalous lack of resources to deal with children who are victims of child abuse, sexual abuse and with those who perpetrate these terrible acts, as well as the adult survivors of abuse. I would call upon this Parliament and this Government to work toward, as our next priority, an end to the scandalous underfunding in this area and to recognize that we have no greater obligation than to assure Canada's children that they will grow up in an environment free from all forms of abuse, including poverty, neglect, hunger, homelessness as well as that of physical and sexual abuse.
We in our Party welcome the proposals and we will be continuing to call, as my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) has called for for some time now, for effective action in the other areas that I have mentioned.

speechtext:
Briefly, if 1 may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to remind Hon. Members of the main features of Bill C-41, an Act to amend the Judges Act, the Federal Court Act and the Tax Court of Canada Act.
Bill C-41 makes four major amendments to these acts. First, it substitutes the industrial aggregate for the industrial composite with respect to the formula established under Section 19.1 of the Judges Act to calculate the annual indexation of the salary of judges. As Hon. Members would know, the industrial composite is no longer published and Statistics Canada officials have recommended that it be replaced by the industrial aggregate.
Second, it sets at 75 the retirement age of all federally appointed judges, in keeping with the requirements of Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms Section 15. At the present

June 23, 1987
Judges Act, Federal Court Act, Tax Court Canada Act
time, county and district court judges as well as Federal Court and Tax Court judges must retire at 70, whereas all other federally appointed judges may continue to hold office until age 75.
Third, it makes a correlative amendment to the provisions concerning a judge who elects to be supernumerary. A judge who so decides may accept a lighter caseload and still be entitled to the same salary and the same benefits. Henceforth all judges will have two options: act as supernumeraries after having attained seventy years of age if they have held judicial office for at least ten years, or after having attained age 65 if they have held judicial office for at least fifteen years. The latter option is now the only one open to judges who must retire at age 70.
And, fourth, it provides that district and county court judges will hold office in the same capacity as their colleagues who sit on provincial superior courts, the Federal Court, or the Supreme Court of Canada. In future all these judges may be removed only by the Governor General on address of the Senate and the House of Commons. Pursuant to Charter Section 15, the Bill is intended to promote equality among federally appointed judges. It does not seem normal that people we have chosen to implement the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms on our behalf should continue to be subject to a different removal procedure and different rules concerning retirement. Mr. Speaker, these are the main amendments contained in this measure. Hopefully the Bill will now pass the third reading stage immediately.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on the occasion of the third reading of Bill C-41 to briefly indicate our support for the legislation and to take this opportunity to raise a couple of points that I believe are of concern, points with respect to the judiciary and the process of the appointment of judges in Canada.
Over a year ago, the then Minister of Justice, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), made a commitment. He recognized that the current system for the appointment of the judiciary in Canada was not satisfactory, was not good enough. The Canadian Bar Association had established a special committee which found that there were serious weaknesses in the judicial appointment process in Canada. It found that in a number of provinces partisan political considerations played a major role in the appointment of judges. Naturally, this tends to bring the judiciary and the process of the appointment of judges under a cloud, particularly in those provinces in which this is the case.
That commitment was made by the then Minister of Justice well over a year ago. The Government has still not moved on it. The Hon. Member for St. John's West, who is now the Minister of Transport, made that promise in February of 1986. His successor as Minister of Justice made a similar promise to the Canadian Bar Association in March of this year. He said that changes would be made to the judicial appointments process very soon.

Mr. Speaker, I see again in the House the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Gerin) and I know quite well that he will agree when I say that we need fundamental changes in the way Canadian judges are appointed. Mr. Speaker, I must recognize that the Hon. Member has used high pressure tactics with the Government and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) to force the Government to keep its promises. Unfortunately, the Hon. Member for Megantic- Compton-Stanstead (Mr. Gerin) has not yet succeeded, together with his colleagues, in making sure that the Government will keep its promises.
Mr. Speaker, I know that there are a great many Quebec Conservative Members who want changes. There was an election quite recently, and the Hon. Member for Richelieu (Mr. Plamondon) nearly won. He almost succeeded, but the forces of the Conservative establishment managed to overcome. But it sent a very serious message to the Government.
June 23, 1987

You should hear the voices of Quebec Conservative Members when they ask for basic changes for instance in political party contributions and especially the system for appointing judges.
I commend the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Gerin), but I also ask him why the Government turned a deaf ear not only to him and his colleagues from Quebec, but to the Canadian Bar as well. They said it is about time we cleaned up the appointment system. I hope the Government will finally keep its promise and bring forward changes to that system.
I also want to take this opportunity to call upon the Government to move forward quickly with the establishment of a judicial education centre. Given the responsibilities of our judiciary with respect to the Charter of Rights, it is very important that they update their knowledge of how they impact on women, native people and minorities. Certainly a judicial education centre would go a long way towards fulfilling that important need.
It is also very important that the Government take further steps to ensure that our judiciary reflect the multicultural reality of Canada. There should be far more women, representatives of visible minorities and natives appointed as judges. Yes, the Government has taken some steps in this direction but it should be taking far more. It should do so by consultation with those individuals and groups who have knowledge and expertise in this area with respect to establishing a new system. That is the spirit in which I call upon the Government to make changes in the process.
Finally, a word about judges' salaries. The Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General recently adopted, by a split vote, a motion approving the recommendations made by the special committee struck to look into remuneration of judges. That special committee was chaired by Donald Guthrie. It recommended very substantial increases. We recognize that the judiciary must be well paid. But I said in committee, and I say again today, that the proposal was excessive. We are not prepared to co-operate in the passage of legislation that would dramatically increase judges' remuneration as proposed in that report. Judges' salaries were increased very significantly just recently and they are indexed to the cost of living. Each year they receive an increase, as do Members of Parliament. I do not believe a case has been made for the kind of lavish increases proposed.
We are told there are lawyers who actually turn down appointments to the Bench because they will not make enough money. The average salary of a federally-appointed judge is something like $105,000 a year. They have one of the most generous pension plans in the country. They have the prestige and status that comes with an appointment to the Bench. They do not have the pressures of operating a law practice. I think they are adequately compensated, certainly comparable to
The Constitution
judges in countries like Britain, the U.S. and elsewhere. I do not want a judge on the Bench who is motivated solely by the desire for more money. If a lawyer is going to say he or she is not prepared to accept $105,000, he or she wants $120,000 or $130,000, I do not want that man or women on the Bench. I want judges there who will serve, having recognized the honour the appointment brings.
One other point with respect to judicial pensions. The current provisions of the judicial pension scheme do not provide for a partial pension after judges have served on the Bench for at least 10 years. One recommendation made by the Guthrie committee that we should look very closely at is that judges who have served for 10 or more years but fewer than 15 receive a retroactive pension. I believe this provision should be made retroactive so that those judges, such as former Justice Thomas Berger, who have performed such a distinguished service for the country on the Bench, will not be denied the pension they have rightly earned.
In conclusion, I am pleased to have had the opportunity on third reading of this legislation to raise these concerns, particularly with respect to the failure of the Government to move forward on changes to the appointment process. I would hope that before June 30 the Government will respond to the very strong representations made by the Bar Association and les reformistes dans le caucus conservateur du Quebec, and that we will see the changes the Government promised.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a matter of significant importance to the people of the Province of Newfoundland and Labrador, and in particular the adherents of the Pentecostal faith in that province. According to StatsCan reports, there are 37,450 such adherents in my province. That could easily have doubled by this time because their number is expanding rapidly.
The purpose of this resolution is to enshrine the educational rights of the people of the Pentecostal faith in my province in the Constitution. In other words, to entrench in the Constitution the right of the Pentecostal Assemblies in Newfoundland and Labrador to operate schools and receive a share of public funds for that purpose. They have had that right in provincial legislation since I think 1954. However, that right was not enshrined in the Constitution because, of course, it had not been recognized in 1949 when we became part of Canada. It has not been covered by Term 17 of the Terms of Union of Newfoundland with Canada.
The educational system of Newfoundland is denominational. This is based on our historic experience in Newfoundland. Education was first provided by various religious bodies. We have had a denominational educational system throughout our history and it continues today. I venture the opinion that this system is favoured by the vast majority of the people of Newfoundland.
At this time we have three educational systems. The first is the integrated system which is comprised primarily of the people of the Anglican faith, the United Church of Canada, and the Salvation Army. That system is operated by the Integrated Educational Council, the President of which is the Reverend Ian Wishart of St. John's. We have the Catholic Education Council which is headed by His Grace Archbishop Penney which looks after the schools of the Roman Catholic denomination in Newfoundland. Finally, we have the Pentecostal Educational Council, the head of which is Pastor Roy King, which looks after the Pentecostal schools in Newfoundland.
In the opinion of those who are knowledgeable in these matters, all three of these bodies are doing fine work in
administering our schools. The funding, for the most part, is public funding from the Province of Newfoundland and Labrador. In addition, as in all educational systems, a great deal of time and effort is expended free of charge by the ministers, priests and nuns of the churches which I have mentioned. I think they are all to be congratulated for this public service and they deserve our support.
If the House passes this resolution, as I am sure it will, this will be a very significant day for the people of the Pentecostal faith in the Province of Newfoundland and Labrador. The resolution would authorize Her Excellency the Governor General to issue a proclamation which will amend Term 17 of the Terms of Union of Newfoundland with Canada set out in the Schedule to the Newfoundland Act.
It is a historic occasion also because this resolution proposes the adoption of the first amendment to the Terms of Union of Newfoundland with Canada. The resolution has been put forth at the request of the Government of Newfoundland, as you might well imagine, Mr. Speaker.

As you know, Mr. Speaker, the Terms of Union of Newfoundland with Canada are part and parcel of the Canadian Constitution, but they apply only to the province of Newfoundland. So, under Section 43 of the Constitution Act, 1982, the Terms of Union of Newfoundland with Canada can only be amended by proclamation issued by the Governor General under the Great Seal of Canada where so authorized by resolutions of the Senate, the House of Commons and the Newfoundland Legislative Assembly.

This resolution affects the Canadian Constitution only as it applies to Newfoundland and it originates with the Government of Newfoundland. On April 10 the House of Assembly of Newfoundland adopted a resolution to amend Term 17 in terms identical to those now before the House.
The Government of Canada is happy to assist the Government of the Province of Newfoundland to achieve these objectives in a manner which basically falls within the jurisdiction of Newfoundland. Education is a matter under the jurisdiction of the Province. We are helping the Government of Newfoundland to rectify a situation which it considers inequitable.
Not only does the Government of Newfoundland consider it inequitable. I, Members of our Party and, I am sure, other Members in the House of Commons consider this situation to be inequitable and will be happy to join us in ensuring that Pentecostal people are treated in exactly the same manner as are those who belong to other denominations in the province. An inequality exists because the educational rights of the Pentecostal Assemblies are not yet constitutionally guaranteed. I mentioned the number of people who are affected by that. There are quite likely in excess of 37,400 at the present time.
June 23, 1987

Through this measure we are enshrining in the Constitution the equality of the Pentecostal Assemblies of Newfoundland with the other recognized religious groups which enjoy status now on educational matters under Term 17 of the Terms of Union.
As a historical footnote, Mr. Speaker, at the time of union in 1949, there were seven denominations specifically authorized by the law of Newfoundland to operate denominational schools and entitled to share in public funds for that purpose. These were the Anglican, Roman Catholic, United, Presbyterian and Congregational Churches, the Salvation Army and the Seventh Day Adventists. Term 17 entrenched these rights as they existed at the time of union and with respect to the denominations then enjoying those rights.
Term 17 of the Terms of Union was a substitute for Section 93 of the Constitution Act, 1867, as it ratified the adoption of the system of denominational schools in Newfoundland. I will not read that section. Anyone who wishes may look at Term 17 of the Terms of Union.
After union in 1954, the Pentecostal Assemblies were recognized under provincial law as being organized for educational purposes. They have been treated that way ever since but have not had the protection of Term 17 for the reasons I mentioned. There is a continuing desire by the Pentecostal Assemblies to be put in a position constitutionally similar to that of other recognized school-operating denominations, hence the resolution now before the Elouse.
You will see that the main provision of the resolution aims at amending Term 17 and provides:
(2) For the purposes of paragraph one of this Term, the Pentecostal Assemblies of Newfoundland have in Newfoundland all the same rights and privileges with respect to denominational schools and denominational colleges as any other class or classes of persons had by law in Newfoundland at the date of Union, and the words "all such schools" in paragraph (a) of paragraph one of this Term and the words "all such colleges" in paragraph (b) of paragraph one of this Term include, respectively, the schools and the colleges of the Pentecostal Assemblies of Newfoundland.
This will, of course, give them the same constitutional rights as now held by the other recognized denominations.
In order to take into account the proposed amendment, the resolution also proposes that Section 3 of the Newfoundland Act be amended to provide:
(2) A reference to this Act, or a reference to the Terms of Union of Newfoundland with Canada set out in the Schedule to this Act, shall be deemed to include a reference to any amendments thereto.
The proposed amendment does not purport to create new rights for the Pentecostal Assemblies of Newfoundland, but to entrench those rights which they already have with respect to education under provincial law. Once again, the amendment does not alter the rights which students belonging to any unrecognized group have under the law of Newfoundland to attend Pentecostal schools.
I am sure that Members of the House, regardless of their political affiliation, will recognize the importance of this
The Constitution
amendment requested by the Province of Newfoundland. 1 am also convinced that they will join forces with us in helping Newfoundland achieve its objectives in a matter which falls under its jurisdiction. I spoke to Premier Peckford this morning and told him that we would be debating this matter today. I believe that with the consent of the opposition Parties we will pass this resolution through all stages today.
It has been a distinct honour and privilege to move this on behalf of the Pentecostal people of Newfoundland. I see the Members for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker), Bonavista- Trinity-Conception (Mr. Johnson) and Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) here to support this motion.

Mr. Speaker, La sexualite blessee, a study published by the provincial shelter association, makes a number of horrifying revelations on sexual abuse in the home. The results of this study clearly demonstrate the link between pornography and violent sexual behaviour.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT SUPPORTED FOR FIRST DEGREE MURDER
REINSTATEMENT SUPPORTED FOR FIRST DEGREE MURDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I support the death penalty for murderers convicted beyond the shadow of a doubt of deliberately planning and killing another human being.
Abolitionists who use Donald Marshall as an example of executing the wrong person are misleading the people as he was convicted on circumstantial evidence only. Under this motion he would in no way be executed. When they say a court is committing murder when a judge sentences a first degree murderer to die, is complete folly. It is tantamount to saying that a judge is a thief when he convicts a person of stealing. Such wild statements undermine our whole system of justice which is based on appropriate punishment for crimes committed.
Capital punishment is not a matter of revenge or statistics. Some can prove or disprove anything with figures. Executing a murderer like Olson, for example, is not half as repugnant as was the raping and clubbing to death of young boys and girls, or forcing a beautiful young girl like Kelly Cook to do "God knows what" and then chaining her to rocks and sinking her to the bottom of a lake.
If we claim to be civilized it is time to think more about the innocent people murdered, the victims and their loved ones, and less about the murderers. Christ showed compassion, but he did not stop the execution of a man whose crime was far less than that of a cold-blooded murderer.

subtopic: SECOND ANNIVERSARY OF AIR INDIA CRASH-PROSECUTION OF PERPETRATORS URGED
SECOND ANNIVERSARY OF AIR INDIA CRASH-PROSECUTION OF PERPETRATORS URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, most Canadians can all too readily remember the horrifying explosion which occurred on Air India flight 182 on June 23, 1985, two years ago today. Three hundred and twenty-nine innocent men, women, and children perished because some deranged person or persons placed a bomb on the plane before it left Canada.
I was in Ireland this time last year with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). We participated in a benediction of a special memorial on the seaside of Dunmanus Bay, 200 miles from the site where flight 182 plunged into the cold, grey Atlantic Ocean.
I can still remember the grief in the eyes and the hearts of the more than 200 relatives from India and Canada who were at that extremely emotional service.
Many walked to the shores of Dunmanus Bay and waded into the sea, in a sense to be closer to their relatives. Some placed flower petals in the sea and watched the flowers drift outward toward the site of the crash.
Moments like this should galvanize the Government's resolve to find and prosecute the individuals responsible. Also, special studies such as the one initiated by Senator Kelly on terrorism may help to prevent soul destroying incidents like this in the future.

subtopic: SECOND ANNIVERSARY OF AIR INDIA CRASH-CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
SECOND ANNIVERSARY OF AIR INDIA CRASH-CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today marks the second anniversary of one of the saddest moments in Canadian history. On June 23, 1985, 329 men, women, and children, most of whom were Canadian citizens, perished when flight 182 was blown out of the sky off the coast of Ireland by a terrorist bomb. It was the largest and most hideous mass murder ever in Canadian history. All Canadians were shocked by the unspeakable brutality of this terrorist act. We mourn the loss of so many of our fellow countrymen, and we share the sorrow of the surviving family members.
We owe it to the victims and relatives of the Air India tragedy to bring those responsible for this vicious crime to justice. It has been two years now, and charges have not yet been laid. All Canadians have a right to know why this investigation was so badly bungled by the RCMP, the Canadian Security and Intelligence Service, and the Government itself.
The time for dithering has passed. We cannot tolerate any more excuses or delays. The Government of Canada has a moral responsibility to establish a royal commission of inquiry into the Air India disaster.
The Irish Government and the Indian Government have both had their public inquiries. We need a public inquiry here in Canada, not only to investigate this terrorist act but also to inquire into the conduct of the Government itself.
June 23, 1987

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF THIRD TERMINAL AT LESTER B. PEARSON INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT
CONSTRUCTION OF THIRD TERMINAL AT LESTER B. PEARSON INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week as a preamble to a question I attempted to tell the House how the great riding of Mississauga North had benefited under Conservative policies since 1984. subtopic: SECOND ANNIVERSARY OF AIR INDIA CRASH-DELAYS IN INVESTIGATION
SECOND ANNIVERSARY OF AIR INDIA CRASH-DELAYS IN INVESTIGATION
speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is of course quite wrong.
He's one of yours!

Yes, indeed, he is a member of the government Party. I am just saying that he is quite wrong.
My undertaking as a First Minister pursuant to Meech Lake is in the 1987 Constitutional Accord which states:
The Prime Minister of Canada will lay or cause to be laid before the Senate and House of Commons, and the first ministers of the provinces will lay or cause to be laid before their legislative assemblies, as soon as possible, a resolution, in the form appended hereto-
The resolution in the form appended thereto is the agreement agreed upon by all First Ministers.
In regard to the question yesterday which I was asked by a very distinguished member of the gallery, I said:

As far as I am concerned, I have no hesitation in suggesting that the Meech Lake Accord is an impressive document that tends to reaffirm Canadian unity. And I have no hesitation in recommending that document to the country and to Hon. Members in this House.
June 23, 1987

Now, our democratic, parliamentary usage provides for participation, something I approve entirely. And we will see what will come out of it, in terms of the Parliamentary Committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pat Carney (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising on an urgent and important question of privilege. The actions of a Member of this House have seriously impaired my ability to discharge my duties and responsibilities as a Member of Parliament. I am referring, of course, to the despicable and irresponsible actions by the Leader of the New Democratic Party in calling me a liar a few feet outside this Chamber yesterday afternoon.
Privilege-Miss Carney
The facts are these. Yesterday, the Leader of the New Democratic Party rose on a question of privilege to claim this Government had misled him and the House on the matter of the Canada-U.S. Auto Pact being included in the present free trade negotiations. You will remember that, in your wisdom, Mr. Speaker, you ruled that the Member had no question of privilege.
Not content with that ruling, Mr. Speaker, and showing contempt for this House, the Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) walked a few feet outside the Chamber and said to reporters, and I quote, "I think she's lying to us about the Auto Pact", as reported in today's Ottawa Citizen. The Toronto Sun reported that the NDP Leader said I was, and I quote, "lying".
Of course, he must be aware of the fact that in making these charges without the protection of Parliament he is exposing himself to the possibility of legal action. In fact, the only person who has ever called for changes in the Auto Pact in this House is the Hon. Member.
I have been asked repeatedly in this House, Mr. Speaker, whether the Auto Pact is on the table, and I replied to the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray):
Canada does not intend to put the Auto Pact on the table. We believe, as I have told the House, that it is working well. If the Americans wish to make any proposals, which they have not yet done, we will look at them. If they increase employment, increase production, and increase investment in Canada, we will look at them.
As you will recall from the rest of Question Period yesterday, Mr. Speaker, members of the opposition Parties continued to question me about the Auto Pact and whether or not it was being negotiated. They based their questions on a third-hand report, a press report of a memorandum written by a congressional staffer in Washington purporting to interpret an oral briefing by the Deputy Chief Negotiator for the United States. That report, Mr. Speaker, has been called into question by no less an authority than the Chief Negotiator for the U.S., who has publicly characterized it as containing "a lot of inaccuracies". Others at the same Washington briefing hold far different interpretations of what was said.
Despite that, the Leader of the New Democratic Party has put this forward as the etched-in-stone American position. The Chief U.S. Negotiator has backed up my statement that the Auto Pact is not on the table. Despite all of this evidence, and my word that the Pact is not on the table, the Leader of the New Democratic Party has damaged my ability to discharge my duties by calling me a liar.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that there have been precedents when statements made outside the House have been determined not to constitute questions of privilege. However, I feel strongly in this case, and so suggest to you, that the behaviour of the Leader of the New Democratic Party, which would be unacceptable and certainly a question of privilege had it taken

June 23, 1987
Privilege-Miss Carney
place in the Chamber, is just as obnoxious, just as despicable, and just as damaging in the lobby of the House.
If you find, Mr. Speaker, that there is a prima facie case of privilege, I would be prepared to move the appropriate motion to refer the matter to the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure.

Mr. Speaker, in response to the Minister's suggestion that there is a prima facie case of privilege, let me say right at the outset that she knows, of course, that there isn't the slightest case of privilege about something that occurs outside the House. She has-

speechtext: " Go ahead, lady"! Sexism raises its head. The NDP and sexism.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
As Hon. Members know, and as the public would be interested in knowing, there is an application before the Chair by the Hon. Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) to the effect that her privileges, her capacity to carry out her duties as a Member of Parliament, have been abridged by the fact that the Hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), has allegedly said of her outside of this Chamber, but within the precincts of Parliament, that she was lying or was a liar. That is the issue. The specific issue before the Chair is, first of all, whether or not those words were used of the Minister and whether their
use just outside this Chamber constitutes a question of privilege.

You have.
The Minister, having made her accusation, I note is leaving the House in a great huff.

Members have many responsibilities in carrying out their duties and serving their constituents. It may be that the Hon. Minister has to leave for some other engagement. speechtext: The Chair recognizes the Hon. Member for Oshawa. I assure the Hon. Member that I shall listen carefully to his intervention.

Minister tried to leave with the House.

Secondly, the Minister went on-and I say, in this context, not simply throughout yesterday's Question Period, but throughout many previous Question Periods, as indeed she has done outside of the House-to play what I call, without any hesitation, linguistic games. I was not interested in the Minister, either inside the House or outside the House, saying that she did not have the Auto Pact on the negotiating table when in fact what she had on the table were the tariff policies which are the guts and essence of the Auto Pact, and the Minister knows that.

misleading the people of Canada on this issue, not me. I believe that profoundly, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not what you said outside. Show a little courage.
I want to conclude with my point-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Tell us what you said outside.
1 want to conclude with the specific-
Be honest.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade

speechtext: I know there are some Hon. Members who would wish this particular matter was over. It will be over sooner if they would keep their comments to themselves.

subtopic: MOTOR VEHICLE TRANSPORT ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, June 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Crosbie that Bill C-19, an Act respecting motor vehicle transport by extra-provincial undertakings, be read the third time and passed.

subtopic: MOTOR VEHICLE TRANSPORT ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will continue from where I left off the other night.
June 23, 1987

Another issue worthy of elaboration concerns the equal treatment of truckers on both sides of the Canada-U.S. border. In 1982, the United States imposed a moratorium on the issuing of licences to Canadian truckers. The power to reimpose the moratorium remains in the United States law and, in addition, a Bill now before Congress would reinforce and extend this power.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) and this Government believe that if Canadian truckers are treated unfairly in the U.S.A., Canada should be able to reciprocate against American truckers in this country. Thanks to an amendment approved by the Standing Committee on Transport, Bill C-19 will provide the Governor in Council with this countervailing power.
Given the close economic relationship between the two countries, we do not anticipate that this power will ever need to be invoked, but we are enacting a regulatory regime that is meant to stand the test of time.
Thus, Bill C-19 represents good, responsive legislation. It has been improved through changes suggested by carrier and shipper consultations, by witnesses who appeared before the standing committee earlier this year, and by the provincial Governments.
When Bill C-19 is enacted, both shippers and carriers will benefit. There will be less economic regulation through the elimination of the public convenience and necessity entry test. The move to reverse onus by January 1, 1988 will mean that only those applications of major importance will go to a public hearing. This will result in less need for costly legal services and a considerable saving for truckers.
The remaining restrictions on rates and routes to be served will be gradually eliminated. This will give both shippers and carriers more flexibility to tailor price and service packages to meet their respective needs and circumstances. As a result of lower costs and innovation, Canadians will have a trucking system that achieves the best service at the best price. This is vital to our economic well being. Jobs-real, permanent jobs- will be created in every region of the country as our producers become more competitive.
The Government of Canada has demonstrated much flexibility in developing and modifying the economic reforms in Bill C-19, but its commitment to safety has never wavered. Safety is the first priority, and this Government has initiated major improvements in the regulation of safety in every mode of transportation. For the trucking industry, the federal and provincial Governments and industry representatives have cooperated to produce a uniform national safety code.
While this Bill was in the committee stage, the federal and provincial Governments reached an agreement on implementation and cost sharing. The code now has a concrete existence. All Governments are committed to implementing it and key
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
components will be in place in federal regulations when this Bill comes into force on January 1, 1988.
The Government of Canada will assist in funding implementation of the National Safety Code to a maximum of $23.5 million over the next five years. We will contribute 100 per cent of the development costs for new initiatives under the Code and 100 per cent of the costs of the information exchange system. We will also contribute up to $250,000 per year per province toward additional operating costs for the first five years.
For their part, the provinces have promised to spend an additional $6 million per year over the same time period to improve enforcement. Of course, these are merely the incremental costs. For example, the provinces will hire new enforcement officers and re-train existing ones as necessary. I understand that the number of commercial vehicle enforcement officers, approximately 1,400, will be increased by 10 per cent. This is in addition to the thousands of provincial and municipal traffic officers who routinely enforce safety on our highways.
The National Safety Code will form the basis of safety regulation in future. Several key elements of the code will be included in the federal safety regulations. The detailed standards for these regulations will be finalized by August, 1987. Hence, once this Bill is passed, federal regulations setting out safety requirements for both trucks and buses will be in place by January 1, 1988.
This should not be misconstrued to mean that we have no highway safety at this time. Canada has an excellent safety record, but we are determined to improve it. We already have a fine regime of safety regulation in each of the provinces and territories. Indeed, most of the elements of the new safety code are already in place in one or more provinces.
Provincial safety regulations are in place now to control driver qualifications and medical standards. All provinces have joined the North American Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance which sets standards for roadside inspections of trucks and buses. Increased roadside enforcement has already started in some provinces and other provinces will follow suit this summer.
There will be improvements made to safety standards in provincial regulations, some of which will be ready by January, 1988 and the remainder of which will be ready by mid-1989. The provinces have made a commitment to have enforcement resources with regard to these improvements in place by the end of 1989.
Over all, Mr. Speaker, the improvements which we will have under the new safety code and Bill C-19 include first, a safety requirement for obtaining an operation licence. For the first time in legislation, all applicants for an extra-provincial trucking licence will have to meet tough safety standards. Fegally, the National Safety Code will be adopted in regulation under the new Motor Vehicle Transport Act and under

June 23, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
the laws of each province. Second, there will be uniformity among the provinces. The code will provide the basis for ensuring that safety requirements for all extra-provincial traffic are the same in every province. Third, there will be information exchange among the provinces. Records on safety deficiencies by companies and individual drivers will be kept and available to all provinces. This means we will have a national enforcement scheme. Work has already commenced to create the required national computer network.
In addition, existing national safety programs for driver testing and control, vehicle safety enforcement and insurance and dangerous goods legislation will be augmented by the following new initiatives to be implemented on or before January 1, 1988: First, upgrading the single driver licensing system, which has been in place for 20 years, to enhance enforcement and control; second, standardization of existing licensing classification; third, modification of existing medical standards for drivers; fourth, modification of existing regulations for security of loads; fifth, a new training course for dangerous goods trainers; and sixth, integration of the Canada Vehicle Safety Alliance with its American counterpart to ensure uniformity throughout North America to the greatest possible degree.
This last initiative is very significant because it will provide a uniform roadside vehicle inspection program. All provinces have signed memberships and paid their dues to the North American organization. As Members from Quebec probably know, a pilot project for safety inspections is being undertaken in that province. This program is already having a positive impact on truck safety in that province. Other provinces are expected to follow suit with similar projects of their own.
Finally, uniform vehicle maintenance standards are being developed as part of the code and will be enforced across Canada by October 1988. Hours of service regulations will be fully enforced by January 1989 and the interprovincial exchange of records will be fully implemented by December, 1988.
Governments, both federal and provincial, the carriers and their employees are all participating in these initiatives to ensure that Canada achieves the highest practicable standards in accordance with the policy statement of the new National Transportation Act, Bill C-18, which we have been considering.
Regarding administration of the code, it makes good sense from all viewpoints to leave it with the provinces which have clear jurisdiction over highway safety. It has been noted, however, that nowhere in law is there a delegation of off-the-road safety practices of extra-provincial trucking and bus companies. We have, therefore, added a section to Bill C-19 which would enable provincial enforcement of safety in the federal jurisdiction.
The time has come for change. The costs of trucking service can be held down, in some cases lowered, by reducing the regulatory restrictions on entry, rates and routes. Both the
federal and provincial Governments are confident that the Canadian trucking industry has matured. It is fully capable of meeting the challenge of greater competition that will result from Bill C-19 and competition with all other modes. Without a doubt, a solid foundation is being laid for long-term healthy growth, both in the trucking industry and in the economies of all the regions of Canada.
There will be a significant improvement in highway safety through promulgation of uniform safety regulations, both federally and provincially and through enforcement by the provinces. We are enacting a regime that seeks to advance the interests of all Canadians by removing obstacles to the growth of our economy and our trade. This legislation will permit enterprise to flourish in the trucking industry, safeguarded but not oppressed by government regulation.
The experience of other countries indicates that the greatest benefit of reducing economic regulation is innovation. It is not possible to predict exactly how it will occur, but free from restrictions transportation companies will develop innovative new services and rate structures. Shippers can then take advantage of these innovations to become more competitive in their markets and jobs are thereby protected or created throughout the economy.
Of course, these benefits will not arise overnight. We are planning and laying the foundation for long-term economic growth. Similarly, there will be no drastic upheaval in trucking services, no destructive, super-heated competition. Why? Because the approach to reform has been thoughtful and balanced with a view to ensuring gradual adaptation.
We stand before a clear window opportunity. The need for the reforms in Bill C-19 is clear, as are the significant longterm benefits for all Canadians in every region of the country. Now is the time to act. Canada is maturing as a nation in transportation.
