subtopic: MOTOR VEHICLE TRANSPORT ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on third reading of Bill C-19, an Act respecting motor vehicle transport by extra-provincial undertakings.
This Bill, which has raised some perfectly legitimate and normal fears in the Canadian trucking industry and elsewhere, will replace the Motor Vehicle Transport Act. When the initial legislation dealing with this sector was adopted in 1964, the federal Government at the time had decided to delegate to the provinces its authority to regulate extra-provincial truck leasing services.
The main consequence of this legislation was that over the years, the provinces adopted a different regulatory framework with widely varying rules and administrative procedures for regulating market entry, abandonment of services, and the setting of rates in the extra-provincial trucking sector. Obviously, we as Liberal Members of the Opposition found cause to rejoice when in 1985, the Government announced it had reached an agreement with the provinces on the general structure of what was to be a new system for regulating extraprovincial trucking, a system that would be more uniform and less cumbersome.
Unfortunately, the proposed legislation arising from this agreement leaves much to be desired. That is why many operators, owners, representatives and experts in the trucking industry are asking some serious questions about the changes introduced by the Government through this Bill. They wonder with good reason why, when dealing with such a major piece of legislation which could change the very nature of the trucking industry in Quebec, the Conservative Government refused to pay any heed to the quite legitimate requests of those who are more familiar than anyone else with this industry. As in the case of Bill C-18, the Government listened only to the organizations controlled by the large and wealthy shippers.
We believe that the Government should have used a much more careful and responsible approach. In preparing a Bill
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
with such a major impact, the Government should have taken care to evaluate the consequences of this measure on such things as road safety, unfair pricing and competition from American supercarriers.
During the next few minutes, Mr. Speaker, I shall attempt to draw a picture of the consequences passage of Bill C-19 by this House will have. We no longer have any choice. The Government has pushed us and speeded up the process to make us agree at any costs, whatever the consequences, to Bill C-19, in spite of the deep opposition of all those involved in the trucking industry in Canada.
For those who did not have the privilege of attending the proceedings of the Committee on Transport, I would like to examine some of the most striking submissions we heard in the committee to underline how unreasonable and even dangerous this Government's initiative could prove to be. First, let us deal for a few minutes with the issue which, perhaps more than any other, gives Canadians cause for concern when we speak about deregulating the trucking industry, and that is road safety. This is the fundamental issue which worries everyone. Once again, we find ourselves faced with a Bill which is the result of the bad habit the Conservative Government has of wanting to imitate the United States in everything. I would even say in this case that the American model is viewed as the ideal of perfection by the Conservatives.

Indeed, in everything it does, the Tory Government seems to be reaching for the American dream. It wants to emulate the Americans in everything, at any cost, even if in some cases it means repeating tragic mistakes. One such mistake would be to go the way of the American Motor Carrier Act of 1980 which, like this Government's Bill C-19, had the effect of eliminating the public convenience and necessity entry criteria, leaving only the question of whether or not an applicant was fit, willing and able.
[ Translation]
Looking at what is going on in the United States under deregulation, we realize it led to an increase in road accidents, increased bankruptcies and concentration into the hands of a few large carriers that conquered new markets through price discrimination. The hard-nosed approach that seems to be favoured by economic advisors to the Minister of Transport takes on a quite different look when confronted to the stark reality experienced by truckers.

That unfortunate tendency in the Department and in the office of the Minister of Transport, of wanting to reduce what is essentially the human condition to mathematical equations, telling us of gain for shippers, must in fact be looked at in light of human suffering. It must be looked at in light of lives lost on the highways because of trucks which cannot economically be maintained any longer. It must be looked at in light of the health of drivers which is jeopardized by taking pills in order to be able to work longer hours. That is the harsh reality of

June 23, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
deregulation. That is the human reality and no number of economy models will make it go away.

But why such a legislation? Why do you find it so terrible, so bad, you might ask?
What the Bill does is open the door to increased competition in an already saturated market. Because what Bill C-19 does is drop the criteria for entry into the market, the so-called public convenience and necessity rule. That criteria, which has been in place since 1954, puts the onus of proof on the applicant. In order to have a chance to get a licence, the applicant must show that the proposed service is needed and the general public will benefit. Only carriers who supply a service that is required and needed get a licence. But under the guise of increasing competition, this Conservative Government decided to change everything, to replace the public convenience criteria by what is now called the "fit, willing and able" criteria. That new criteria is aimed at allowing any business, whether large or small, that proposes to operate an extraprovincial trucking service and that meets minimal standards-I am not referring to maximum standards, because now they are lowering that down to the most minimal of standards, the least common denominator in terms of safety and insurance-to get a licence almost automatically, as a matter of course.
The Government says that in order to meet provincial and industry concerns, the Bill provides for a five-year transitional period for moving from the current system to a so-called capacity system.
However, Mr. Speaker, a closer look at Bill C-19 proves this to be a scam.
During this interim five-year period when what is called a reverse onus test will be applied amounts to de facto deregulation. It is interesting to listen to what the Canadian Trucking Association had to say on this issue:
Based on all the legal advice available the CTA Board is convinced that the reverse onus language in Section 7 of Bill C-19 is useless to achieve the purpose supposedly intended of providing a transitional mechanism.
The reverse onus concept in C-19 amounts to subterfuge in terms of any transitional protection. That is because: The approach removes virtually all discretion from provincial boards.
Following the U.S. example, the change to a totally new test must lead to a deluge of early applications that will swamp the process before it can be properly tested.
The prospect must be that the new language will sooner or later result in court challenges thereby tying up the interpretation of the concept indefinitely in the courts.
It can be easily circumvented by carriers acquiring existing operating licences of which there will soon be a glut with minimal, if any, review mechanism applicable.

Because that new criterion reverses the burden of proof to licence holders, who will now have to prove that the entry of a new carrier on a route that is already served will endanger the service's profitability. The difference between that test and the previous one is quite clear: under the new system, anyone owning a truck will get a licence if he is fit, willing and able.
The repercussions of that increased competition on road safety is a matter of upmost concern to us and to the trucking industry. Because it is clear that safety considerations cannot be examined or perceived independently from a specific, economic context.
Let me quote on this the excellent brief submitted by the Ontario Trucking Association to the Committee on Transport, in March 1987.

Safety considerations cannot be separated from economic regulatory reform. We know this is not the intent of the Government of Canada. However, this point needs to be emphasized. There is a direct relationship between economic deregulation and highway safety. Faced with increased competitive pressures and declining profitability, some carriers will-in a deregulated environment-be forced to give less than adequate consideration to those factors which ensure public safety. Costs will be cut in those areas most related to safety-proper vehicle maintenance, inspection and replacement procedures, driver training and operational control. An October 1986 study of road accidents involving heavy trucks in eastern Quebec, points to implications arising from the impact of deregulation on independent truckers or owner-operators.
A 1986 U.S. study conducted by Transportation Research and Marketing in conjunction with the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance also reported some shocking results. The study's 100,000 interviews showed that average speeds of trucks increased sharply following deregulation from 60 m.p.h. in the 1977-79 period to about 65 m.p.h. in the 1983-86 period. The study also showed that the average age of equipment rose from 3.7 years in the initial period to 5.2 years in 1986.
In the struggle for traffic, some owner-operators will be forced to run excessive hours and over-exploit their equipment. All of these factors endanger the lives of motorists and truckers alike. Experience in Australia and California has demonstrated that the economic ills resulting from deregulation put some carriers' commitment to safety under extreme pressure.

Often, Mr. Speaker, both during the second stage debate on Bill C-19 and during the hearings of the Standing Committee on Transport, we, of the Liberal Party, have indicated just how concerned we are about the consequences deregulation will have on highway safety.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) and the Conservative Members kept repeating that we were raising a nonproblem. They felt that there was no connection between highway transport deregulation and the deterioration of safety experienced in the United States.

That attitude shows either a sign of intellectual dishonesty or a disquieting lack of homework on this crucial issue, on the part of the Minister, his officials, and Conservative members of the committee.
June 23, 1987

Indeed, let us look at the California experiment with deregulation. The California Public Utilities Commission has been recently looking to reinstate some basic rate regulation, finding that to be in the public interest. The factors causing the C.P.U.C. to reintroduce rate regulation was a deterioration in safety. Of course, the one explanatory variable was deregulation. To quote from this brief:
Since 1980, when California deregulated the intra-state trucking industry, the following has occurred:
1.	Public Safety-By 1983, years of steady improvement in truck safety statistics has reversed. The truck accident rate per million miles has skyrocketed by 22 per cent between 1983 and 1985.
2.	Employee Safety-The workers' compensation rate for trucking company employees increased by 44 per cent between 1978 and 1985. It is currently 51 per cent more than comparable industries.
3.	Safety Expenses-Since deregulation, the California trucking industry is spending 10 per cent less on vehicle maintenance and repair even though truck fleets have aged.
4.	Safety Practices-Since deregulation, support of the trucking industry for the Certified Practising Safety Administrator program and the annual Safety Congress has dropped by 83 per cent and 49 per cent, respectively.
Of course, it is evident that the California situation differs somewhat from Canada. No two jurisdictions are totally alike, obviously. However, we have to look at the empirical evidence from California, and that is undisputable. Ignoring these facts is a sign of irresponsibility of the worst kind.
We in the Liberal Party who have opposed this legislation cannot understand why the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), who now has the experience of the U.S., is proceeding so rapidly and so urgently without taking the appropriate precautions.

The Government's failure to recognize facts which are not consistent with its wishes will have characterized its approach from the very beginning. It demonstrates that the deregulation which the Conservative Government is proposing is a purely ideological exercise.
It is quite unfortunate that for ideological considerations and to please the powerful lobby of major shippers, this Conservative Government is prepared to jeopardize the safety on our highways. I do not hesitate to say that it is prepared to risk the lives not only of our truckers, but also of each and every person who travels on Canadian roads.
As far as safety is concerned, the American experience is quite convincing, as I mentioned quite briefly in the document which I have just submitted and which is quite clear. But in case it is not, I should like, if I may, to quote another source.

Allow me to quote from a booklet prepared by The Coalition for Sound General Freight Trucking which is made up of motor carriers, shippers and other persons concerned about the future of the general freight trucking industry in the U.S:
In the case of the independent owner-operator, it means hauling a load for whatever price can be had. Sometimes, this is bare, out-of-pocket money for
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
operating expenses and perhaps some contribution towards the monthly equipment loan and something to send home to the family; sometimes it is nothing more than fuel money to get back to a more promising source of loads.
It also may mean speeding or making the cross-country trip with little or no rest because only by maximizing the number of hauls per month can the financial obligations be met. It also may mean choosing what to do with the limited cash inpocket: fuel for the trip, meals, money sent home, or brake relining or adjusting. Not surprisingly, maintenance is the first to go.
This type of experience is frightening. We cannot understand why the Minister wants to ignore it.
Let me now cite another study which was prepared by Professor Glaskowsky. In a chapter on safety and equipment aging it says the following:
Opponents of deregulation predict trouble in regard to safety deterioration due to the aging of equipment and financial pressures to defer maintenance. Trends since 1980 clearly confirm this prediction.
The American Trucking Association, Inc., in its March 19, 1986 statement before the House Subcommittee on Surface Transportation, summarized an increasingly serious trucking safety situation as follows:
1.	Truck accidents reports to the Bureau of Motor Carrier Safety increased 18 per cent in 1984. That is the largest increase since 1972.
2.	Trucks placed out of service by federal and state inspectors for serious defects increased from 23 per cent in 1984 to 41 per cent in a national truck inspection in September, 1985.
3.	The per centage of motor carriers with unsatisfactory safety ratings is highest among those that have recently received operating authority from the Interstate Commerce Commission, and the number of these new carriers is steadily increasing.
4.	Unsatisfactory safety ratings are more prevalent among motor carriers with smaller profit margins.

I think that the impact which deregulation will have on highway safety is quite clear. And I do not think that we could honestly disregard everything that is done, said and written about the negative effects of deregulation in the United States.
Unfortunately, that is the path this Conservative Government has chosen. Because of this and because of the great many facts which the Conservative Government has overlooked, we are quite concerned about the welfare and safety of those men and women who drive the juggernauts of the highway; we want our highways to be as safe as possible, and we say that the Government's will to go ahead with deregulation before the implementation of a national highway safety code is altogether unthinkable, inconceivable and unacceptable. The Official Opposition has been essentially asking the Government, in view of the American experience, to realize that it cannot go ahead with deregulation in Canada as long as there is no national highway safety code in place, and as long as the Provincial and Federal Governments have not hired properly trained inspectors in sufficient number to ensure that our highways are safe; until then, it should not implement Bill C-19.

June 23, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
I should like to quote also from the excellent brief submitted by the Quebec Trucking Association which provided another testimony which the Government should have listened to.
Recognizing the value of a single rule for all, you assured us that you understood the problem and that the introduction of the regulatory reform would coincide with the coming into force of a national safety code imposing the same standards to all. We were also given the assurance that the means to enforce that code would be provided. We were assured that a control mechanism regarding enforcement of and compliance with all social and fiscal obligations imposed on the trucking industry would be implemented. We were finally assured that we would be able to compete with foreign trucking companies on an equal basis.
Where do we stand now? The Government wants to deregulate as of January 1st, 1988, but nothing indicates that we could have a uniform safety code throughout Canada before 1990-91. Each province looks at its role in this area in its own way and the only national leadership is the wish to agree on some uniform code at some indefinite time. You can imagine what the situation will be if anyone can start a trucking business without proficiency or fitness test, without rules or control mechanisms for things like vehicle safety to protect the general interest of the public
What we cannot understand in particular is the desire of the Government to move in a direction that the Americans are starting to abandon. When you look at what happened in the United States after deregulation you see an increase in traffic accidents, a rising rate of bankruptcies, and a greater concentration of the industry, where a few firms have been able to gain new markets through discriminatous, pricing and other means. The cost-benefit analysis takes an entirely new aspect when we compare the benefits of the shippers to the direct and indirect costs incurred in other areas such as accidents caused by vehicles in bad repair, the health of drivers who take drugs to work longer hours, etc. California was the first state to get into deregulation, it is also the first where steps have been taken to restore regulation.
Evidently, the Quebec Trucking Association is concerned by what the Tory Government is trying to do and in this paper it is trying to slow down this deregulation process. The Liberal Party believes that it is essential to proceed with caution before embarking in that dangerous course of deregulation of motor vehicle transport. This is the reason why we introduced an amendment in committee, both during consideration of the bill clause by clause and in the House at the report stage, amendment which tied the implementation of Bill C-19 to the setting up of a national security code. Unfortunately, in his eagerness to serve the interests of a few large Canadian shippers, the Government has overlooked the most elementary carefulness and common sense.

The Government is in fact telling Canadians that it does not care what is happening in the United States, it does not even seriously address their arguments and concerns but will deregulate immediately and worry about safety later. That kind of attitude is unacceptable. Also unacceptable is the staggered implementation schedule for the 17 components of the safety code to which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) has agreed.
On some components compliance is not estimated before August, 1989. On the absolutely crucial question of hours of service enforcement, four provinces and two territories will not bring their regimes in until, at the earliest, May, 1989.
Of course, we are talking here of estimated compliance dates. The Minister has no guarantee as to the implementation of the safety code. Yet he proceeds with full deregulation. We
think the Minister should have waited for an effective and enforceable national safety code to be in place before proceeding. To please his powerful shipper friends, he has put the cart before the horse and, in so doing, is jeopardizing safety on our roads.
[ Translation]
Notwithstanding all the minister's fine words in committee and in this House to the effect that security is and will always be the main concern of his government, a mere cursory examination of the facts shows that there is reason for concern. On that basis alone, Mr. Speaker, we would have voted against this legislation. But there is more to it than that.
We will dwell a while upon another issue that concerns the trucking industry in Canada, that is the unfair price practices that result from a deregulated system. It is perfectly clear that in a free market where competition prevails, the shippers will tend to look for the lowest rate available. According to the most basic rules of deregulation, that would be one of the big assets.
Yet we must be careful. Testimony before the California Public Utilities Commission in February, 1987, provides significant insight into the dangers of unfettered price competition. Volume discounts and rate reduction had become the order of the day in California. Several carriers have not had any increase at all in their rate levels since 1980.
Moreover, a price floor has never been achieved in California. Some carriers have always been willing to cut their rates to get a shipment. Indeed, transportation is like a perishable product, a missed load could never be recaptured. That seems to be the prevalent philosophy in California. I suggest that that could be the prevalent philosophy in Canada if we proceed with Bill C-19.

In our opinion, accepting Bill C-19 as is would have catastrophic results for the Canadian motor vehicle transport industry. Most certainly, the American industry giants will be among the first to ask for licences that will have become easier to get. According to industry members in Canada, foreign takeovers of Canadian road carriers will multiply within five years. Since 1981, operating costs in Canada have increased by 28 per cent. That comes mainly from taxes on gas and outrageous costs of liability insurance.
In the same period, the loading rates have increased by only 5 per cent. The net result is that the profit margin has dropped 3 per cent to become one of the lowest since the Second World War. So the large American firms, whose sales often surpass those of the entire Canadian industry, will be in a position to easily penetrate Canadian markets, to lower their rates, to offer predatory prices, to absorb some losses for a year or two and then to take over any Canadian truck undertaking in
June 23, 1987

difficulty. This is why it is dangerous to introduce such an entrance requirement when profit margins are at 3 per cent; the Canadian trucking industry could be destroyed.
Here again, on the question of unfair practices, the American experience teaches us that caution should be the rule, given that, since the coming into force of the U.S. Motor Carrier Act of 1980, which marked the beginning of the deregulation process in the American trucking industry, the largest firms have been growing constantly. In fact, the four major firms, Roadway Express, Consolidated Freightways, Yellowfreight and United Parcel Services, have increased their share of the American market by 24 per cent. This figure demonstrates clearly that these companies intend to increase their market share and can do it rapidly.

These predatory practices by American carriers have been highlighted by the recent anti-trust suit filed by Lifschultz Fast Freight, a motor carrier based in New York, against the three largest American motor carriers in the United States, Consolidated Freightways Motor Freight, Yellow Freight System and Roadway Express.
Let me quote from the American Transport Association magazine Transportation Topics, from May 18:
Three of the nation's largest trucking companies asked a Federal Court to dismiss an anti-trust law suit filed against them by another carrier.
Lifschultz Fast Freight of New York filed the suit March 3, seeking over $1 billion in treble damages from Consolidated Freightways Motor Freight, Yellow Freight System, and Roadway Express. Lifschultz alleged that the fleets attempted to use predatory pricing to drive competitors out of markets and obtain control of those markets. The three carriers were accused of doubling their combined market share in the general freight LTL market over the last ten years at the expense of 104 other carriers Lifschultz said were driven out of business through a concerted campaign of predatory pricing.

Mr. Speaker, in a deregulated market where only the strong survive, the heavyweights can take advantage of their superior strength. By opening Canada's doors wide to these companies, the Government may see the same situation develop in this county, and I think the risk is even greater, because as we know, the American Anti-Trust Act has a lot more clout than the Canadian Competition Act. Despite recent amendments to our Competition Act, I have I am very much afraid that the big American companies will be able to come and do here what they are now doing in the United States and do it even more easily in Canada, because the Competition Act will not have the necessary clout to take on these companies and prevent them from abusing market forces and engaging in unfair competition with small Canadian truckers.
When the Conservative Government justifies its policy by saying that the legislation make the sector more competitive, I think we should remember that the bulk of that competition will come from the giant companies south of our borders, and that Canadian companies will be hard pressed to survive.

Our main concern is that the legislation on combines investigations will not have enough clout to prevent this kind of unfair competition.

In the whole history of the provision which dates back to the 1950s, only six cases have come to the courts, only one conviction has been obtained and that was for goods given away in large quantities for a period of one year.
The reasons for such ineffectiveness are clear. Predatory pricing is a criminal versus civil offence under the Competition Act. All elements of the offence must be satisfied by the criminal standard of proof which is proof beyond a reasonable doubt, and all criminal law defences are available, including the Charter. The predatory pricing inquiry into Canadian newspapers was launched in 1978 and is a good example of what I am talking about.
Marshalling sufficient evidence to meet the criminal standard of proof is very difficult and is the reason most often cited by the Director of Combines for discontinuing inquiries. The courts have said that the evidence must be strong to convince them to intervene and convict.
Indeed, as Mr. Moore, in his book How Much Price Competition said: "The battle is likely to be over before the case is completed". Such a situation is dangerous for our trucking industries.
We recognized this and at the report stage the Liberal Party moved an amendment which, in some small measure, dealt with these very real concerns. Of course, government Members voted it down, and that is regrettable. It is regrettable because I feel that the Bill deals inadequately with this very serious situation that could arise.
In conclusion, I want to deal with the third area of practical concern which is tied to the use of predatory practices from American mega-firms.

The U.S. companies tend to be bigger and more monolithic, for the very simple reason that a dynamic infrastructure connecting urban centres to terminal networks, set up many years ago by the trucking companies, makes for a very efficient system and, more important, a system that works strongly in favour of the U.S. industry with respect to its ability to compete with the Canadian trucking industry.
In the United States, a network of as many as 860 highways connects metropolitan markets of over one million people. In meagre contrast, Canada has only three. Furthermore, the widening gap between our two taxation systems as a result of the major reforms introduced in the United States in 1986 is working to the advantage of the U.S. companies. They pay less income tax, proportionally, because of the way tax reform has affected vehicle depreciation in the United States. American companies pay a lot less tax on gas, and there is far less government intervention in the U.S. in labour-management

June 23, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
relations. All these factors tend to make Canadian companies less competitive.
During the debate at the report stage, we expressed the hope that the Minister of Finance, when tabling his White Paper on tax reform, would take this opportunity to consider the serious problems facing the Canadian trucking industry.

Unfortunately, that was not to be the case. Indeed, there was, for example, no recognition that the Canadian trucking industry was particularly susceptible to U.S. competition and, therefore, ought to have been looked at outside of the larger corporate picture.

On the same subject, I would like to quote from a document sent by Mr. Ken MacLaren of the Canadian Trucking Association to all members of the Standing Committee on Transport:

If anything, the capital costs allowance comparison information on trucking understates that true advantage of U.S. truckers. Under recent U.S. corporate tax reform a U.S. trucker can now write off heavy duty tractors (Which are by far the most expensive item used in international highway transport) in only three years, not five years as shown in the example.
The attached information was released by Mr. Tom Younan of Price Waterhouse at the CTA conference on tax reform at which Mr. Younan shared the platform with Parliamentary Finance Committee Chairman Don Blenkarn. During the same conference, Lana Batts, Vice President, Policy of American Trucking Associations, in addressing the same audience, referred to the fact that by far the most important gain made by U.S. truckers since deregulation has been under tax reform.
The U.S. trucking industry's relative tax position has been dramatically improved. At one point the U.S. trucking industry was the most heavily taxed industry in America.
From the standpoint of the Canadian trucker, a ten to twenty per cent differential in after-tax return coupled with significantly higher capital cost allowance provisions in the U.S. could be enough to persuade at least some Canadian truckers that the time has come to relocate their international operations. Some are doing so already. Certainly that would be the case if Mr. Wilson follows through on previous indications that he intends to reduce CCA rates.
The Canadian Trucking Association had also asked that compensation for loss of value of operating authority be based on the fuel tax formula base developed for those truckers who could not claim under the existing tax write-offs for good will. There, too, the White Paper was silent.

Mr. Speaker, if the Government had any sense at all, it would rethink its strategy. It is letting an industry that employs 50,000 Canadians... Its 50,000 workers earn an honest living, and their lives are about to be disrupted by the deregulation of the transport industry in Canada. Their jobs are being threatened by the Canadian Government's desire to act quickly. The carelessness of the Canadian Government
could mean a slow but certain death for the Canadian trucking industry.
I therefore believe that this Government is acting quite irresponsibly in trying to further the interests of the big Canadian shippers who have asked for these changes and in jeopardizing the existence, the safety and the very life of many truckers.
The Government might destroy by one stroke of the pen what several generations have given us by building a strong and competitive trucking industry.
Of course, the coalition of shippers wants deregulation. However, just as obviously, Canadian truckers are opposed to it.
In closing, I would like to point out that the Government and the Minister have no guarantee from the provinces that a road safety code will be implemented next year or the following year, or even early in the next decade.
We are therefore going to have to approve in 1987 a piece of legislation which has been imposed to Parliament by the Conservative majority and which will completely deregulate the trucking industry in Canada in the hope that, within the next three or four years, there will not be too many accidents or too many abuses in the system and that, in the early nineties, an adequate road safety code will have been implemented.
In my opinion, the Minister of Transport is acting irresponsibly. He has abandoned all sense of his public responsibilities in forcing us to give passage to this Bill in spite of all the warnings he has had and in spite of the disastrous experience of the United States trucking with deregulation.
The Minister of Transport is acting irresponsibly, and as I pointed out in the case of Bill C-18, within a few years, we in the Opposition will have to repair the damage done and amend this piece of legislation in the interests of truckers, workers in the industry and the Canadian public.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been for a number of years that I have had the opportunity to involve myself in the whole question of deregulation of the trucking industry. As a Member of the Ontario Legislature from 1975 to 1977, I participated in select committee study within the Province of Ontario on possible deregulation, and since being elected to the House of Commons in 1984, as a member of the Standing Committee on Transport, first dealing with Freedom to Move and then with Bill C-18 and Bill C-19, the twin deregulation Bills of this Government, I find that much of my political life has been caught up in the study of trucking and the rules which apply to it.
I want to say at the outset that I regret seeing once again a Conservative Government-I regret seeing a Conservative Government at any time, actually-moving federally in the same way as it did in Ontario to change the rules of the road.
June 23, 1987

Before I get into the specifics of the Bill, I would like to quote part of a speech given by the President of the Public Utilities Commission in Idaho earlier this year. An article reporting on the speech is entitled "Idaho PUC President Swisher Dubs Deregulation 'Free-market Feeding Frenzy"'. I think the manner in which this gentleman approaches the whole concept of deregulation is interesting. Those who are watching and those who will be reading Hansard for this day's debate will find the speech most interesting. Mr. Swisher said in his speech:
"Utter deregulation is a leap of faith if it can actually be carried off," Idaho Public Utilities Commission President Perry Swisher told a national conference of utility executives and regulators recently.
Swisher was on a panel addressing the topic of total deregulation of the telecommunications industry. The panel was part of the Third Annual Current Issues Conference organized by the Center for Public Utilities at New Mexico State University's College of Business Administration and Economics.
"For about eight years I've been hearing testimony from gurus who proclaim, and interviewing biz ad and econ graduates who believe, they have found God in the market," Swisher said. "The marketplace, if unfettered, will cure warts."
Swisher characterized the drive toward deregulation of the nation's utilities as a proto-religious movement.
"An incredible foundation of this new creed-when you consider the prosaic halls where it is taught-is its Book of Genesis," he said. "In the beginning, there was a free market in which all transactions occurred, in innocence. Enter government, the snake, with regulation, the apple. I stand before you as an heir and beneficiary of a profound seduction. Do away with my function-I myself need only be reduced to a consultant, not a beheaded corpse-and paradise will be regained.
"No other society has this mythology. It is uniquely American-
And I might say North American-
-like jazz. Unlike jazz, but very like the hula hoop and aluminum siding and dental floss, it will last as long as it entertains, preoccupies, and fills a service as yet unprovided by a higher technology. That is, it is oboriginal.
"What we learn is that the entirety of regulation can't be dismantled, if only because some freedoms-as distinct from liberty-rely on regulation," Swisher said. "Freedom of the road would be even more dangerous than it is if your choice of a driving lane on a two-way street was entirely up to you and whether you prefer to stop at green or at red lights, the same. Ideological fervor for flat-out deregulation is of a part with anarchy. It is romantic in the extreme.
"Where deregulation has occurred, it has taken two primary forms," Swisher said. "One is the preemption of local or state authority by federal fiat. The other consists of displacing public, impliedly consensual regulation with private, strategic regulation. Nearly all deregulation has commingled these two strains."
Swisher cited transportation "deregulation" for examples. Idaho's two pages of in-state rail tariffs have been replaced by 150 pages of Interstate Commerce Commission rules. Even so, railroad management now has more freedom. One result has been the abandonment of hundreds of miles of Idaho branch lines.
"-ore concentrates, for example, now go by truck 110 miles to the railhead, paralleling for most of that way a rusting bed of deserted track," he said.
"Nationwide, that energy-efficient system for moving freight is on the decline. Non-metropolitan access is declining. In yet another generation, American rail deregulation could eventuate in the nationalization of the railbeds-a gift from the free-market ideologues to the 21st century, and all in the name of free enterprise.
"Trunk airlines served four, sometimes five airports in our state of scarcely a million people, before deregulation. Now they serve one-Boise. Dozens of
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
Idaho communities lost scheduled common-carrier truck service with truck deregulation. Greyhound crosses Idaho only for the reason a chicken crosses the road-to get to the other side-
"How long the free-market feeding frenzy will last, of course I don't know. Not long, I hope, because it is oblivious to real-world consequences."
In a nutshell, this gentleman has given us the concept and how it is perceived by some people. I would now like to turn to the Bill.
As we worked through Bill C-19 in committee we tried to sow the seeds of doubt in the minds of government Members on the committee. More than that, we tried to sow the seeds of doubt in the minds of officials from the Ministry, from the Minister's office and from the regulatory agency. They are the ones who shape the legislation for the government of the day. We tried to sow doubt in their minds in order to bring about some changes to try to make what we consider a bad Bill a slightly better Bill.
As you yourself know, Mr. Speaker, given your role in the committee, there have been some changes. For the most part we welcome those changes. We wish that the amendments that we had put forward had been accepted in their entirety both in committee and in the House. But, unfortunately, the might of the Government was against us. One could suggest that the might of the bureaucrats was also against us.
It is interesting to note that during the run-up to third reading of Bill C-19 the argument was that this was a shippers' Bill, that it was out to redress some imbalance that existed in the system so that the shipper, the individual who produces a commodity and wants to get it from point x to point y, would get a break because of this Bill. The shippers were strong in their lobby. Their lobbied members of the Opposition, members of the Government, the Minister and officials. They used public platforms wherever they could find them to put forward their case.
On the other side was the trucking industry. Obviously, for vested reasons, and I do not say that in a negative way, it was concerned about the impact of this Bill on its ability to survive and to operate.
So we had two opposing camps. I know that the Shipping Council of Canada was quite upset with what it perceived to be backroom manoeuvering. While we were out on the road as a committee, the Transport Committee having been given the task of reviewing the Bill clause by clause, deals were being made in the Minister's office between truckers and the provinces, the truckers and the federal Government, or between the provinces and the federal Government.
When the shippers appeared before us again in Montreal, I said: "Welcome to the real world of politics". I said that because, unfortunately, that is how things go, deals are made. The shippers now find themselves very unhappy with the Bill. As opposed to their original suggestion to pass the Bill quickly they now feel that damage has been done to the Bill by changing the three years reverse onus provision to five years. It no longer meets their needs. They are now suggesting that it

June 23, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
should not go forward. They are appealing to us for a last minute change that would reverse the decision that was made in the backroom between the trucking associations and the Government.
Ironically, while we welcome this new-found opposition, we have said all along that reverse onus is just a form of deregulation and that for all intents and purposes, whether it is three years or five years, deregulation will happen overnight. It will happen as soon as this Bill is proclaimed, as soon as we go to the fit, willing and able test instead of the public convenience and necessity test.
I cite for Hon. Members the experience on the air side where we have had a modified form of deregulation since the spring of 1984. It was brought in by the Minister of Transport of the day through a policy statement. It put in place the reverse onus stipulation so that there is no real strong reason for carriers to object to a new entrant.
We had a situation back a year or so ago in which Air Ontario was coming in to run parallel to Air Canada on a run from Thunder Bay to Sault Ste. Marie or Sudbury, I am not sure which. I went to the local manager and asked: "Are you guys opposing this?" He said: "No, because opposition these days to that kind of thing just does not work, the regulatory agency is not listening to us any more".
If Bill C-19 passes in its current form-and we will do what we can to prevent it from passing-the moment it is proclaimed, which will probably be January of 1988, there will be deregulation in the trucking sector.
Let me go over some of the concerns that we on this side of the House have. We are concerned about safety, about employment, about service to the small communities and the small shippers. We are worried about the decisions that a lot of these new carriers are going to have to make.
If a small one-man operation or family-owned business is faced with the choice of making the bank payment on the rig or buying a needed set of tires, the bank manager will get his money. The small operator, faced with payments that are due and a family to feed, will take the chance on his tires lasting one more week, or his brakes lasting one more week. And because he has on his mind the next payment on his rig and the need to do something about his tires or his brakes, he will push himself as well. He will take an extra hour or two on the road; he will hustle for that extra load he can get by driving 300 miles out of his way.
Faced with a broker who tells him that he has a load if he can deliver it that night, he will take that load. He will stretch himself and his equipment in order to keep food on the table, in order to keep the rig on the road, and in order to keep the bank manager from his door.
That is the kind of scenario we are worried about. We know that the "Sears" of the world, the "Canadian Tires" of the
world are not going to be cutting corners in that way. Such corporations have the ability to cross-subsidize within their operations. On the air side, we do not worry about Air Canada or Canadian Airlines International. It is the little guy that we are worried about. We are worried about the small operation, the one-man or family-owned company which does not have a stable economic operation such that it does not have to cut corners. Once corners are cut, safety is jeopardized.
In the United States, we have seen a massive disruption in jobs. We have seen a loss of jobs and job displacement. We have seen a real attack on unionization and a real attack on union wages.
We are concerned about the small communities. In a regulated environment, if a trucker applies to serve two large centres, the provincial regulatory boards are in a position to grant such a licence on the condition that a certain level of service be provided the smaller communities in between. For example, the communities along the north shore of Lake Superior cannot, in and of themselves, justify large volume transporters in or out; they are, however, accessible if a trucking firm, wishing a licence to serve the major centres on either end of the north shore, is instructed to provide service.
We are concerned that once Bill C-19 is passed, it will not be possible to exert the kind of regulatory pressure necessary to force transport companies to provide service to such communities. Everything will be reduced to economies of scale. It is the bottom line that will dictate the level of service.
During committee consideration of the Bill, the trucking companies and shippers indicated that it is the small communities which will be the losers; that it will be the small communities which will face reductions in service, or possibly elimination of service; that it will be the small communities that will face increased tariffs.
In the regulated environment, the carrier was assured a reasonable return in respect of services provided to the smaller communities. Under a free market system, with no control over prices or service, the fly-by-nighter could come in and undercut the existing carrier, driving that carrier out of the market, out of the community, leaving the community in the unregulated hands of that new carrier, a carrier which is quite prepared to squeeze that community for every penny it can because it knows there is no competition.
That is the ultimate irony of this Bill, as it is the ultimate irony of this Government. It professes a belief in competition. Yet, this legislation will eventually-and I emphasize "eventually"-mean less competition.
We have seen that take place in the United States, as we have seen it in other modes in Canada. On the air side, we are back to two major carriers. The little guys have either been gobbled up or have themselves gobbled up the big guys. Where is the competition?
June 23, 1987

We in Thunder Bay do not even get advantage of seat sales. Because there is no competition other than the two major carriers, we lose out.
I should like to go back to the safety aspect for a moment, Mr. Speaker, because it is that aspect that is really of concern to us. Recognizing the inevitability of the passage of this Bill, what we endeavoured to do in committee was to ensure that the necessary safety tools were in place and operational for at least one year before we moved from the "public convenience and necessity" test to the "fit, willing and able" test.
Fit, willing and able means that if one has the money to buy the truck and pay for the insurance, one gets the licence. One's banker becomes one's regulator. If the banker feels that he is a safe risk financially, he will get money. There is no guarantee of long-term stability. It is just that he has enough money to buy the rig, to pay for the licence, to put in some gas, and perhaps to hire an employee or two. That is all the banker looks at. As long as the owner keeps paying the loan payments on his truck and whatever else he has, the banker does not really care what happens.
We tried to convince the Government that there should be a delay, that at least a year should pass. We know the situation today under a regulated environment. The Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) sat through the committee hearings with us. With his personal political history in Alberta, he knows that things are not that great out there today. We have a lot of unsafe trucks on the road. We already have a lot of corner cutting. It is our feeling that we must bring that up to an acceptable level before we change the rules, so to speak.
We heard evidence from the Province of British Columbia which had conducted a number of safety checks, both local and province-wide. They basically shut down sections of the highway and either pulled everyone over or every fourth or fifth operator. I would like to give an indication of the kinds of things that were found. I refer to an April 5, 1987 article which appeared in the Vancouver Province entitled "Safety check is shocking". In part it reads:
Only one truck passed a random roadside safety inspection specially staged for The Sunday Province.
And three of the eight trucks given a 33-point check were pulled from the road by the Ministry of Highways area inspector Sam Nair.
"It's always the same things-brakes, steering and tires," says Nair.
"We require that 50 per cent of the brakes be working effectively-some of these trucks are not even meeting that."
Nair confirmed that as many as 80 per cent of trucks stopped have either failing brakes or ones that are not adjusted properly.
We have had a situation in northwestern Ontario where because of the nature of our region we do a lot of logging. We have a lot of off-highway and on-highway haulage of both tree length and cord length wood. I discovered through communications with one of my constituents that under federal law there is no requirement to have brakes on an extra axle.
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
These trucks have an axle which under full load drops down so that they have an extra set of tires to carry the load. The trailers are built with brakes on that axle unit, but the regulation does not require the brakes.

Mr. Speaker, again I thank you for giving me the floor on this Bill dealing with deregulation, specifically in this case the deregulation of motor vehicle transport by extra-provincial undertakings.
Without referring to all the points already raised by my colleagues who have spoken to this Bill, I will lay emphasis on the question of safety because it happens to be my greatest concern, Mr. Speaker: the Minister is going ahead with motor vehicle transport deregulation without first implementing a national safety code. The provinces and the federal Government may very well have signed an agreement a few months

June 23, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
ago, but I firmly believe that the national safety code will not be ready by January 1, 1988 when deregulation takes effect.
As you would know, the Committee on Transport held public hearings throughout Canada, and a number of interest groups took this opportunity to urge us not to proceed with highway transport deregulation until such time as a national safety code has been put in place. These people also sought the assurance that the national safety code would be standard from coast to coast, not a checkerboard code but a code which would be similarly applied throughout the country. If I may, as an example I will quote the Atlantic Provinces Trucking Association which represents the interests of the 300-member trucking industry in the four Atlantic provinces. Here is what they had to say, and I quote:

While the original concerns and/or opportunities presented in the initial brief remain valid today for the most part, the APTA would like to point out that members are still uncertain as to the impact of the various proposed changes. Varying interpretations are being given by federal and provincial officials in such key areas as the timing and enforcement of the new National Safety Code as well as the uniformity of the regulations themselves.
Truckers in the Atlantic provinces are faced with a minimum of five different interpretations of other areas such as the meaning and intent of the "reverse onus ' test in enabling a gradual reform phase and commitments to review the impact of the same on the structure of the trucking industry.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, Members of the House would be interested to know that the APTA's mandate is to promote the well-being of the trucking industry in the Atlantic region. Their views are extremely important, and I should think the Minister would indeed be well advised to take them into account. APTA spokesmen also cautioned the committee Members that the impact of deregulation might be quite different in the Atlantic region as compared with the rest of the country. Again I quote:
"The APTA would also like to point out that regulatory reform in the trucking industry may have a different impact on carriers in the Atlantic provinces compared to other parts of Canada. It is our understanding that many provinces across Canada may continue to regulate intra-provincial freight movements as they have in the past, while adopting freer regulations for interprovincial freight movements. Given the smaller size of the intra-provincial freight markets in the Atlantic region, concern has been expressed as to whether or not present provincial and regional carriers will be able to survive in such an environment".
The above comments apply particularly to the three Maritime provinces which are the three smallest provinces in Canada. Should the scenario be that the National Safety Code regulations and their enforcement not be uniform, and the "reverse onus" tests be interpreted differently in the three Maritime provinces, then considerable havoc could result in trucking operations.

It was also noted that APTA officials did insist on the fact that rail rates had to compensate. They felt strongly that Bill C-18 did not provide adequate guarantees, but that Bill has now passed the third reading stage.
Mr. Speaker, I must point out that the concerns of APTA have not been allayed.
With respect to the national safety code, I should like to read a letter written by Trucking Association President Raymond R. Cope and recently published in newspapers. This rather enlightening article is entitled "Deregulation Safety Threat to Truckers, and I quote:

Deregulation safety threat to truckers.
Transport Minister John C. Crosbie's letter (June 10) suggesting that the implementation timetable for the new National Safety Code is consistent with safe trucking in Canada is totally misleading. The facts are these:
With the passage of Bill C-19, the extra-provincial trucking industry within Canada will be effectively deregulated as of January 1, 1988. Economic regulation of the trucking industry in Canada has in the past provided barriers that have prevented many unsafe trucking operators from acquiring operating authority. Thus, economic regulation has had a safety regulation by-product.
With the elimination of economic regulation, the only barriers to irresponsible trucking operations will be those laws and regulations which are brought into being across Canada to implement the new National Safety Code.
The minister of transport has indicated that the National Safety Code is to be phased in between 1988 and 1990 and that the main elements of the code will likely be in place by January, 1989. This will mean that for the period January 1, 1988 to January 1, 1989, there will be inadequate safeguards to irresponsible and unsafe trucking operations.
As a result, the accident rate in Canada will be higher than it otherwise would be with correspondingly higher numbers of injuries and fatalities.
The deregulation experience in Australia and in the United States has clearly established the need to have a proper safety net in place before the onset of deregulation.
It is essential that the Government of Canada take immediate steps to synchronize the timing of the effective implementation of the National Safety Code and the phase-out of economic deregulation.

And it is signed by Raymond R. Cope, President, Ontario Trucking Association.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian trucking industry is far from being satisfied with Bill C-19. And what about the Canadian people who are quite concerned about the increase in trucking traffic on our highways. Already, we are well aware that the deregulation experience in the United States trucking industry has resulted in a considerable increase in the number of highway accidents.
We, on the Standing Committee on Transport, have been warned by several experts that a similar situation could develop in Canada if a national safety code is not put in place at the same time as deregulation. It is unfortunate for all Canadians, but the Government just will not listen, preferring to risk the lives of Canadians, which is altogether unacceptable.
We, of the Liberal Party, would prefer not to see this bill implemented before the national safety code is in place. We should listen to the officials of the trucking industry. We feel it would be wise to take into account the American experience and to set in place first a national safety code.
To conclude my remarks on highway security, Mr. Speaker,

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to speak on behalf of my Party on this legislation which envisages the almost total deregulation of the trucking industry. Under the government proposals there would be a radical change in the way in which the Canadian trucking industry is structured, organized and operated. The impending cut-throat competition this Bill envisages will permit, and in fact in the view of some of its supporters promote, the elimination of most small and medium-sized firms in Canada. There is also the likelihood of intense market battles with large American-owned companies such as Roadway Services of Ohio, Yellow Freight Systems of Kansas, and Consolidated Freightways of California. They could cut a swath through our industry and this would lead to another essential service being dominated by organizations outside of this country.
I believe there are a number of significant, serious and incontrovertible effects of deregulation. Initially, of course, it can bring more competition. I do not think that point is seriously in doubt because barriers to entry into the industry will come down. It will no longer be essential to go through the sort of application process to get routes, necessary permits and licences, as it once was. This will encourage anyone who has or can borrow sufficient capital to buy a truck or, let it also be said, simply to make a down payment and lease a truck, to get
June 23, 1987

into the industry on the basis of a mom and pop type of operation. A couple of brothers or someone hiring a couple of friends could get in the business. It would of course be nonunionized and vulnerable to all sorts of exploitation and difficulties which can arise in a very small firm that depends for its livelihood on the crumbs off the table of the larger companies.
I believe it to be incontrovertible that within a matter of few years there would be a greater concentration of industrial ownership. The big would get bigger and more American, the medium-sized would go bankrupt or be bought up, and the small would scrap fiercely for the crumbs of local markets. The economic pressures under such a deregulated regime are not going to contribute significantly either to economic prosperity or to social harmony in Canada.
We are fortunate never to have seen what one might almost call civil war which has prevailed from time to time in the American trucking industry largely as a result of moves to deregulation. Rate slashing on the major routes has already begun. Discounts are being offered. I, of course, have no objection to discounts being offered but this relates to the whole theory and practice and, indeed, the differences between the theory and practice, of a competition economy which I will go into in some detail later. Discounts as high as 50 per cent on general freight rates and as high as 20 per cent on commodity rates have been reported. We are seeing an over-capacity that will become even more acute as the large American-owned firms and their subsidiaries enter the market.
Trucking deregulation is, of course, closely tied to the Government's free trade initiative. There is little doubt that an unspoken priority on the Government's agenda is to harmonize, as far as possible, Canadian economic policy and Canadian economic regulation with the regulations of the United States. There may be some transitory benefits from this. There may be some small gain. There may be some savings realized in, of course, the larger markets, the larger centres, and the more powerful industries.
However, what a cost there is in terms of American domination of our industry, in this case our commercial trade trucks rating. What a cost in terms of the often painful adjustment which Canadians may have to go through. What a cost in terms of lost jobs and lost wages for people who find their companies taken over by companies which are not prepared to pay the wage rates that they have won through their unions.
Canadian shippers who, after all, are the industrial sector lobbying the hardest for deregulation, are motivated by that self-perceived need to lower their transport cost to match the deregulated American transport costs in preparation for a continent-wide scramble for markets. Thus we see the tie-in between the Government's free trade initiative and this Bill,
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
which is essentially free trade in trucking initiative which is being foisted on the Canadian people.
Let us not forget that so many of those Canadian shippers are themselves branch plants of American firms. The interests they are serving are not necessarily interests of employment, Canadian production, and reinvestment in Canada but may very well be impelled by a desire to increase the economic return that they can send back to the United States in the form of management fees, royalties, licences, franchise fees, intercorporate dividends, and cross-investment.
The potential for the larger American trucking firms to overwhelm the Canadian industry is so palpably obvious that even the Government economic analysts could not ignore or misidentify it. Each of the six largest American companies holds more freight in a single year than the entire Canadian industry. Indeed, the general manager of the Manitoba Trucking Association has argued that the largest U.S. carrier with dozens of terminals can take over the Canadian market by the simple expedient of serving at cut-rate prices from the addition of perhaps four distribution points.
This gets into the fundamental fallacy of the "free market philosophy" as promoted by the Government and as incorporated and inherent in the ideological agenda which underlies the free trade initiative and whose thoughts, of course, underpin this entire Bill.
The fact is that if there is such a thing as a free and perfectly competitive market, it is yet to be identified, at least on this continent. The fact is that natural forces, not necessarily market forces, but the forces of psychology which are inherent in human behaviour, consistently and continuously militate against that so-called free market, that nirvana which sets Tory ideologists salivating and which yet ever remains beyond their grasp or beyond their practical realization. The fact is, of course, that American trucking, which is what is being implicitly held up as a model to us in this Bill, was for years dominated by forces which could be termed less commercial than collusive, less competitive than collaborative and, very frankly, not contributing to the healthier development of society in the United States of America.
I recall the idea that is set out by Adam Smith in the Wealth of Nations about the perfect competitive market. Yet, in recalling it I am unable to come up with any example from real life that truly offers a parallel which could be identifiable as enshrining and incorporating these free market characteristics. Everywhere the free market is trumpeted to exist there are oligopolies and monopolies and there is predatory competition.
It is very difficult for me to imagine an industry which would be more vulnerable to predatory competition and the use of pricing structures to run the smaller competitors out of business than the trucking industry. Surely this has to be one of the industries in which it would be hardest to regulate such a practice and in which it would be hardest for the small operators to survive the operation of such unfair competitive

June 23, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
practices. The ability of the larger companies to control the generation of any internal evidence that might point to collusion and to eliminate any visible semblance of collaboration must surely be the major vulnerability in this legislation.
Let us see how it works. Take the case of a small trucker newly entered into the business, lured in by the Government's glittering vision of cross-continent market possibilities, of north-south routes. He has gone to his bank manager with perhaps 25 per cent equity or has gone to the leasing company and entered the trucking industry with one or two major clients, one of which is taken away by the operations of a larger competitor.
This person must then start playing the rob-Peter-to-pay-Paul game. He must decide whether to put this month's customer cheque into the lease payment or into new tires or necessary work on the rig he is driving. It is not a pretty picture. It implies that safety will deteriorate. Even the Ontario division chairman of the Canadian Industrial Traffic League, who has supported deregulation, admits that highway safety is likely to get worse under deregulation when profits start to be squeezed.
I have a considerable amount of documentation from studies that have been done in this industry which can be used to back up such a conclusion. Rather than get into the simple reiteration of statistics which I know my colleagues, in their diligence and knowledge, have put on the record already, I would like to point out some of the likely consequences in terms which can perhaps be more vividly imagined and in terms which relate specifically to my riding.
In the United States the highway accident rate is rising, equipment is being kept on the road longer, is being less maintained, and is carrying heavier loads. I can envisage what is likely to happen in my riding with Highway 17, the Trans-Canada Highway as it is officially and somewhat hyperbolically named given the state of maintenance to which it has been allowed to deteriorate. I believe the highway is already in a condition that reflects no credit upon the federal Government or the Government of the Province of Ontario. Given the likely impacts of deregulation on loads and running times over the road, I cannot foresee that the highway will stand up any better.
One loser in deregulation will be the Canadian truck driver. The impact of deregulation upon the American trucker was devastating, since upwards of 300,000 union jobs were lost, major concessions were demanded and benefits were rolled back. If there is one lesson that the economics of this North American continent should have taught all of us by now, it is that the more remote, less prosperous and less economically influential areas of this country are where the severest impact of deregulation will take effect.
My riding contains many areas which might be classified as remote, small centres. In many of these parts, freight comes
from 300 to 400 miles away, generally in truck load form and occasionally in less than a truck load form.
Quite often there is not a back haul for the trucker to return due to the nature of the local economy and the size of the community. Deregulation in these areas could lead to a reduction of service, an increase in prices and, after taking over the medium carrier, abandonment by the larger carriers who may not find the smaller market worth-while any longer.
There are a number of examples in my riding of opposition to this Bill and the Government's over-all deregulation plans. On April 13, 1987, the Town of Fort Frances passed a resolution that the request by the Fort Frances and District Labour Council for the Town of Fort Frances to register opposition to Bills C-18 and C-19 be approved and the request of the District Labour Council be fully supported.
The District Labour Council in Fort Frances compiled an excellent brief and analysis on the possible effect of transportation deregulation in an area such as Fort Frances which is over 200 miles from the nearest major centre.
They were concerned about less competition, about control of the market by fewer firms and, above all, the situation under deregulation where because of dips in profitability over an extended period of time it may not pay the airlines, buses, railways, or trucks in this instance, to routinely provide service to outlying areas. Nothing in the legislation will either compel them to do so or indeed give them any incentive to do so.
As the Labour Council said:
How many of our local businesses will be able to afford the higher price of shipping or receiving their goods, and if the increased costs are passed on to the consumer, how many customers will they lose, if unemployment rises due to business failures, there will be even fewer markets than before. Shrinking markets and higher transportation costs are not factors likely to attract investors to our community.
When we consider deregulation of the trucking industry in my part of northwestern Ontario, we have a powerful example that we believe provides a close comparison and very persuasive paradigm of what may happen. I refer to the airline industry. We have had a spate of amalgamations in the airline industry in this country that have led to a loss of jobs. While there has been some improvement in other areas, it is my experience that there has been a deterioration of some services and our over-all impression is that deregulation is not good for the outlying areas of this country.
If we consider the situation in the United States now, a very persuasive report published in one of our national newspapers a couple of weeks ago indicated the degree of inconvenience and disservice suffered by airline passengers all the way from the downtown taxi terminal to the point of arrival because of the effects of deregulation. A copy of Harper's Index indicated that the average airline fare in the United States since deregulation had risen 42 per cent.
We should not be looking to chaos in Canada's trucking industry any more than the United States should have been
June 23, 1987

looking to chaos in its airline industry, which is the situation that appears very much to be developing. I and my Party stand in opposition to this Bill. It is not the prescription for the development of a healthy decentralized Canadian economy. It is a prescription for more centralization under the control of our neighbours to the south.

They will have the opportunity to either drive that competitor into bankruptcy or purchase the assets of that competitor, often at a very reduced price, and incorporate them into their own wider operation.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the regulations made under the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, in order to repeal the dispositions which have the effect of taking into account severance pay and pension income when assessing unemployment insurance entitlements.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think the chronology of events which has lead to the necessity of my presenting this motion
June 23, 1987

for debate is very essential for us to look at. This motion-and I know that Bill C-50 was passed some weeks ago-is one more attempt to persuade the Government to look into its heart and to see how the passage of the regulations following the announcement in November, 1984, by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) have impacted so unfairly on many, many Canadians. Furthermore, it is another attempt to try to persuade the Government that, in effect, what it passed in Bill C-50 some weeks ago goes only part way in retreating from the untenable position announced by the Minister of Finance in November, 1984.
We all recall November, 1984. The Conservative Government came to power with a massive majority. What did the Minister of Finance state in his first budgetary statement on November 8, 1984? Suddenly, it was not "jobs, jobs, jobs" anymore but it was "cut the deficit, cut the deficit, cut the deficit". There was not any consultation whatsoever with those who were affected. Their representatives were not consulted. Members of Parliament on the government side were not consulted, nor were Members on the opposition side. Members of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration were not consulted. The Unemployment Insurance Commission, which has the responsibility for administering the UI program, was not consulted. The Advisory Council of the Employment and Immigration Commission was not consulted either.
The Minister put on his new shoes, came with his blue rose in his lapel-if one can imagine a blue rose-and stood up in the House and announced changes to the Unemployment Insurance program by which pension income and severance pay would henceforth be considered earned income for unemployment insurance purposes.
From the moment the Minister sat down we on this side of the House condemned his announcement. At that time we said that this treatment of pension-severance pay as earned income was unfair, that it was discriminatory and illogical. We know that over 100,000 Canadians were affected by that announcement. They were negatively affected. The Government saw pension income as earned income.
I want Hon. Members to think about that for a moment. Pension funds are really savings. A worker agrees to take part of his wage and the employer agrees to match it. The money is put aside in a pension fund and can only be withdrawn when the employee reaches a magic age or fulfils the agreement of the pension program.
In small companies which do not have pension plans what does a worker do? Looking to his retirement years, a worker takes part of his income and places it into an RRSP. He may very well make some investments to look after his retirement years so that when he stops working or when he is of an age to leave his job he can withdraw the funds. Yet the RRSPs and the investment income are not affected by this ruling. It is only the pension plan wherein a worker saves for his retirement years that is affected by this regulatory change.
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
One of the things that struck us at that time was that the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, which states that pension income or severance pay was not earned income for unemployment insurance purposes, was an Act of Parliament passed by Members of the House. What the Minister of Finance announced was an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act, and it was done by regulation. It seems to me that that sort of fiat struck at the very heart of what we call parliamentary democracy. In fact, the Government did by stealth what it did not have the courage or the fortitude to put before the House in the proper form as a Bill.
Having taken that position, the proverbial you-know-what hit the fan. In fact, some would say that the Government held up the fan. Having done that, we saw more slipping and sliding than one has ever seen in a stable. The Government backed up and then slipped and slid and postponed until, in fact, it stirred the pot so much that it was impossible to see the bottom.
Nobody knew where they stood in respect of the regulations regarding UI and pension income and UI and severance pay. The former Minister, who is now the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald), kept issuing edicts which postponed the pension change, so what was announced in November 1984 did not become effective until January 5, 1986. When the whole thing was blowing up, to save face and their political necks, they used a good tried and true method-they asked a commission to study the matter.
The matter was turned over to Claude Forget, and the Forget Commission studied the change in respect of pension income and UI. The commission was to make a recommendation to the Government on both the pension question and the severance pay question.
Not only were the changes unfair and discriminatory, but they set up classes. There were those workers who were able to work deals with their employers such as in the case of Inco and Falconbridge in my community where workers could have their pensions deferred for a year while they collected UI. Not all workers, certainly not Armed Forces personnel, are able to make that kind of deal. Therefore, we have one set of workers treated one way and another set of workers treated in an entirely different way.
The Government and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) held up Bill C-50 as their solution to the problem. It even says that a worker can collect full UI benefits provided that he gets a second job. If a worker takes an early retirement, he must show good faith by going out and getting a second job. If he gets a second job and is laid off from it, he can collect his full UI plus his pension from his first job. How discriminatory, how class conscious.
It might be easy in some parts of the country for workers to get second jobs. In places like southern Ontario it is quite possible. However, it is not so easy for older workers to get second jobs in northern Ontario, the Atlantic provinces, British
