Columbia, or parts of the northern Prairies. In fact the Government has reinforced the discriminatory aspects of the original change in 1984.
We know how difficult it is to get a second job. As a matter of fact, the 1985 report of the Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council pointed out that the change in unemployment insurance regulations was seen as a most unfortunate development which came at a time when every means of assisting unemployed older workers should be explored. Even that advisory council pointed out how difficult it was for older workers to get second jobs.
Since the recession of the early 1980s, the whole question of early retirement was used by employers to ease older workers out of the active workforce to protect the jobs of younger workers. That is a fair goal. Many workers accepted it. It is not that they were finished with the work world, but they could go out to seek a second job, knowing full well that they had the backing of unemployment insurance to tide them over. Once they made that decision, they were hit between the eyes by an unconscionable change in the rules. The Government is changing the rules in the middle of the game.
No active player of hockey or any other sport would expect a referee to blow the whistle in the middle of a game and say, "I have just been handed a change of rules by the governors of the league, and you shall not shoot unless you are 60 yards from the goal". No referee would start introducing all sorts of changes in the middle of a game, but that is exactly what the Government did. It did it without any representation from the players in the game or their representatives. It was certainly done without any consultation with Parliament or its standing committees.
What did Claude Forget say when he finally reported? He said to the Government that the idea that pension income was earned income and the changes were fine, but that he disagreed with the way in which they were implemented. He said that the Government had not given enough notice to the players in the game and therefore advised it to go back and pay all the UI and then make an announcement that as of January 5, 1989 the new rules would come into effect.
Of course that is a little fairer than what the Government did, but it is totally unacceptable. Let me make crystal clear that we would not accept that, because using pension income and severance pay as earned income was unfair in the first place. They are savings.
The Minister had that proposal from the Forget Commission. Then the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration looked at the question. I see the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais) in the Chamber; he is the new chairman of the standing committee. It looked at the Forget report and at the pension income and severance pay questions.
What did the standing committee say to the Minister and the Government? It was an all-Party committee and there was
a majority decision, with only one member voting against it. It said that pension income was not to be considered earned income for UI purposes.
Mir. Boudria: Who voted against it?

I say to the Government,"Shame, shame, shame". It is not too late. It is never too late to repent. Just as we passed Bill C-50 by regulation, the Government can change the rule and give pensioners their full UI benefits. It can say to those people who were laid off and got severance pay, "By golly, you take that severance pay and use it, and with the UI benefit get retrained or move to a place where there is a job; use it to tide yourself over until you get another job".
Instead, what did the Government do? It punished them. I see you signalling, Mr. Speaker, that I must wind up. I am just getting going. Can you imagine anything more cruel than a person who has worked 15 years for a company and one Friday he gets a blue slip-it is not pink any more, it is blue-saying "You are through". He gets severance pay of $7,000. This fellow has 15 years with that company. He is not going to walk out of the door of that company and pick up another job because he may be 35 or 40 years old. What do we do? First, we penalize him by making him pay tax on that $7,000 even though he has lost his job. The Government turns around and says to him "You don't get UI benefits because you have $7,000". Is there anything more heartless, cruel, unfeeling and insensitive? I say it is a shame. Shame, shame on the Tories. Shame on them.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak this motion. In fact, in seventeen months this must be the twenty-fifth motion tabled on the subject in the House of Commons. I think Canadians and parliamentarians, especially Conservative Members whose memories tend to be rather short, should recall it all started on January 5, 1986. Before January 5, 1986, if a worker, old or young, lost his job by reason of termination of employment or because he agreed to take early retirement and let a younger person take over his job, as an alternative to laying off people, and if he was then in a position to look for another job, he had the right to draw full unemployment insurance benefits, notwithstanding any income from an employer-employee pension plan or severance pay following the closing of a plant.
Unfortunately, on January 5, 1986, not by a decision adopted in the House of Commons but by regulatory order, supported by Cabinet, including the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), this Government decided-

From then on, after protest movements were organized in Quebec, the Liberal Party, at the request of its Leader (Mr. Turner), got together with these coalitions to force the Government to change its course. At that point, all this Government could say was: Well, we are going to ask the Forget Commission to tell us whether we are right or wrong. And that was because not a single Conservative Member in this House had the guts to tell the Minister: You are wrong. The money belongs to those workers. It's their money. It's the employers' money. It came out of their pockets.
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
The money doesn't belong to the former Minister of Employment and Immigration, the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald), and it doesn't belong to the Prime Minister. It belongs to the workers. The Conservatives said: Forget Forget. If you got your benefits, you will have to pay them back.
Mr. Speaker, not a single Conservative Member rose in the House at that time. Elderly workers had to come here to Parliament Hill to challenge the Government. They were unemployed and they had to spend money to come here. They were losing money every two weeks because the Government didn't give them their full benefits. These people had to pay S20 or $25 to charter a bus and come and challenge the Government because they could not have meetings with their Members in their ridings. There were pressures from the representatives of ARSAC, from Mr. Cloutier, Mrs. Lalande, Mr. Fortin of Montreal, and from representatives of our military. After three manifestations on Parliament Hill and after publication of the Forget Commission Report, the Government was told: "You were wrong; Mr. Prime Minister, you are wrong; you have to reimburse these people; you cannot change the rules in the middle of the game." Did you ever hear of someone who has automobile insurance being told after an accident: "I am sorry, but the rules have changed and you can get compensation only after your second accident. Go and have another accident, and when you lose your other leg, come back and see us; we shall pay you for both." This is silly, but it is what the Conservative Government wanted to do.
We have won half the battle, thanks to the Leader of the Liberal Party, who asked the members of his party to fight as long as something could be done to obtain fair treatment for older workers. Unfortunately, in spite of the pressures exerted by the Official Opposition, by the labour organizations, by the Forget Commission, which cost $6 million of taxpayers' money and whose recommendations were rejected out of hand by the Government, and by the Committee on Employment and Immigration, including its Conservative members, with the exception of the Hon. Member for Jonquiere (Mr. Blackburn)- In passing, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Laprairie (Mr. Jourdenais), even though I cannot congratulate his other colleagues who have been content to do nothing publicly while leading us to believe in private that they were doing something, because he at least was not afraid to defend these workers and to tell the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) and the Prime Minister that they were wrong.
Unfortunately, what the Government has given us is even more shocking than the amounts spent on shoes by the Prime Minister. It is shocking to think that all the workers over 55 who are laid off following the closing of a plant, whether on the South Shore, in the Quebec riding, in the Richelieu riding or anywhere else in Canada, are being told: "My dear sir or madam, you are not entitled to your full unemployment insurance benefits as are other workers because the Conservatives have decided that the pension contributions you paid while you were working is not an investment, but earned

And that is the kind of injustice which this Government and Conservative Members, including the Member for Richelieu (Mr. Plamondon), the Member for Quebec East (Mr. Tremblay) and the Member for Chateauguay (Mr. Lopez), are willing to condone to make sure that all workers who lose their job as a result of a plant closure as well as all military personnel, men and women in our armed forces, who are now needlessly paying unemployment insurance premiums, will have to find alternate employment, and if they should lose that second job then the benefits are no longer deemed to be an income as they were the first time.
This gives you an idea of the way this Government operates and manipulates people. Had it not been for the determination of the Liberal Party, for the doggedness of various groups such as ARSAC, the Quebec coalition and representatives of the military, had it not been for them the 35,000 early retirees in Canada, including 13,000 in Quebec, would not be getting their cheques. Indeed the Government and the Tories were satisfied with the situation, and the only reason why they decided to reimburse these claimants was that we turned the screws on them, we had them with their backs up against the wall and they were ashamed. They are sending refund cheques to these 35,000 people because they have been forced to do so, not because they think these people had a good case.
But we have to be on our toes .. . Mr. Speaker, I have only two minutes left. People have to be on their toes. At the request of my leader, I can assure these people-because the cheques have not been delivered yet-that we will keep an eye on the situation until the last minute, until these 35,000 people get their money.
It does not matter where they live-Quebec, Alberta, the Atlantic Provinces, Western Canada-we Liberal Members have been asked by our leader to be vigilant and make sure that these people are not penalized as a result of this decision.
Mr. Speaker, I conclude on this note and I hope the Conservative Members will rise to speak. I think the New Democratic Party Members have clearly and unequivocally expressed their opposition, no one has to wonder where they stand. To us Liberals the issue is crystal-clear: we want things to be as they were before, we do not want two classes of workers, we do not want any injustice.
Now it will be the Conservative Members' turn to speak, and I hope we are not going to see a lot of twisting and turning and posturing and beating around the bush as we did when the early retirees went to their offices. It seems they said: Well, personally, I think you are right, but you know how things are .. . And once they are back in the House, they switch sides.
Mr. Speaker, I am about to conclude my remarks, and I hope there are some Conservative Members who will fight,
because there is still a chance, there is still a glimmer of hope, a very slight glimmer, if Conservative Members are prepared to take a stand in their caucus and demand that the Government introduce amendments to give all workers a fair deal, instead of just half the early retirees.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to rise in the House during the hour set aside for Private Members' Business, and especially to speak to Motion 26 which deals with Bill C-50, an Act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, which contains, as you probably know, and I think it does no harm to repeat it, three important amendments for Canadian workers. These deal with the provisions to include income from pensions and severance pay in calculating unemployment insurance benefits.
As Hon. Members well know, on April 5 of this year new regulatory provisions dealing with pension income and severance pay came into effect.
One of the amendments contained in Bill C-50 makes amendments dealing with pensions retroactive to January 5, 1986.
Since January 5, 1986, income from pensions arising out of employment is considered as earnings for the purposes of unemployment insurance.
Bill C-50 provides that a worker whose benefit period is based on subsequent employment, whether it started before or after January 5, 1986, will no longer have his income from a pension arising from his previous employment considered as earnings for the purposes of unemployment insurance.
This Government has always held the firm conviction that individuals who retire should not consider unemployment insurance as an additional source of income.
Furthermore, we must make a distinction between people who retire permanently and those who retire in order to start a new career. The amendments allow for this distinction. They make sure that that group of people who retire and start on new careers are treated fairly and equitably, since they are still part of the labour force.
It is our belief that those people should be entitled to full unemployment insurance benefits, whatever their pension income.
Those amendments will benefit workers who have started on a new career in which they pay unemployment insurance contributions. If they later become unemployed, they will be entitled to full unemployment insurance benefits, based on their employment income following retirement, whatever their previous pension income.
In order to illustrate the situation, I will give a real life example taken from the experience of some retirees and the impact on them of the new proposals in the Bill.
June 23, 1987

Let us take a member of the Canadian Forces who retired in February, 1986 and applied for unemployment insurance. Linder the January 5, 1986 regulations, the amount of his pension income will be deducted from his unemployment insurance benefits. No change so far. Let us now assume the same person found a new job in June, 1986 for instance, and was laid off a few months later. Under the previous regulations, they would have kept on deducting his pension income from his U.I. benefits.
Under the provisions of Bill C-50, the worker whose unemployment insurance benefits were reduced because of pension income will be reimbursed all the deductions to that time if his benefit period is based on previous employment.
On the other hand, another major amendment will allow people who filed a claim for unemployment insurance benefits before January 5, 1986, to have their eligibility determined under the old rules. As the saying goes, old claims, old rules.
As already mentioned in this House, some people have allegated that they were given vague information about the pension income provisions which came into effect on January 5, 1986. The fact is that, when the regulations on pension income came into effect, retirees with pension income either lost their entitlement to unemployment insurance benefits or had their benefits reduced.
Bill C-50 therefore provides that any claim filed before January 5, 1986, is not covered by the regulations on pension income.
The eligibility of these claimants will be determined under the old rules. To make this even clearer, let me say that a retiree whose unemployment insurance benefits have been interrupted or reduced because of his pension income and who filed a claim before January 5, 1986, will be reimbursed an amount equal to the deductions from his benefits.
Mr. Speaker, the provisions of Bill C-50 will affect many Canadians. These changes show the determination of this Government to ensure that all workers are treated fairly. As I pointed out in this House on June 11, Mr. Speaker, I shall continue to monitor the progress of this Bill to ensure that it is approved by the Senate as quickly as possible so that the workers concerned can have their cheques shortly.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that we are Firmly convinced that our unemployment insurance legislation now meets the expectations and needs of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to rise in support of the motion before the House put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez). He has fought an incredible battle for fairness and equitable access to unemployment insurance for many Canadians. Wherever I go across Canada, I find that the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt is certainly held
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
in very high esteem because of the job he has done on this particular piece of legislation.
I wish to discuss a matter that affects retiring members of the Canadian Armed Forces. Many individuals have retired in the area of Comox and generally when individuals retire from the Canadian Armed Forces, they are not in a position to choose the time they retire. They are asked at a certain age to leave the Armed Forces in order to make room for younger people or for new people. It is as a result of that that throughout the years, when individuals have left the Armed Forces, they have been able to take with them unemployment insurance benefits in order to make adjustments into the community.
Adjusting into a community is very important because many of these retirees are in their forties and fifties and have to make profound adjustments. Many leave the area in which they had been living. Many must sell homes in which they had lived for some time and must purchase other homes in other areas. This adjustment is hard to make on the rather meagre superannuation they receive immediately upon leaving the Armed Forces. Therefore, it is important that they have unemployment insurance benefits as a cushion to carry them through that adjustment period. Most Canadians would agree that after 20 to 25 years of service to their country, retiring members of the Canadian Armed Forces are entitled to that cushion.
Many of those members have children graduating from high school and going on to post-secondary education. This is a time of enormous financial burden for the families concerned. Not only are they retiring from their lifetime career, they are faced with the additional financial burden involved in their children attending university. If you live in the Comox Valley, your children must travel hundreds of miles to attend university. They have to pay for room and board, tuition, books, and otherwise support themselves. Members of the Canadian Armed Forces who retire to the Comox Valley and wish to support their children who are attending university need the additional cushion in the form of unemployment insurance to make the adjustment. As I said, most fair-minded Canadians would agree that it is not unreasonable that those people receive the benefit of that income.
What has the Government done? In January of 1986 it decided it would no longer permit this to happen. Right in the middle of the game the Government changed the rules. Retiring members of the Armed Forces did their homework. They made preparations. They were in a position to take responsibility for the transition to civilian life. Then, all of a sudden, the Government changes the rules of the game. This has caused great suffering. Many of these people were unable, on such short notice, to make the adjustment to meet their responsibilities. Many of them were unable to obtain employment or, in any case, reasonable employment to fill the gap.

June 23, 1987
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
That will not be quickly forgotten. Many people who supported the Conservatives in the last election thought that they would make right the years of neglect by the Liberals. What happened? They found they were even more badly handled by the Conservative Government.
In addition to being unable to collect unemployment insurance, the Government, adding insult to injury, insists that when they go to work they pay unemployment insurance premiums. Here you have a retired member of the Armed Forces collecting a modest pension, forced to immediately obtain employment because he or she is unable to collect unemployment insurance-and it is often only part-time employment at low wages-and then forced to pay unemployment insurance premiums on top of it all. Given the seasonal nature of work in many areas of British Columbia, particularly in the Comox Valley, lay-offs occur frequently and the individual finds he or she cannot collect unemployment insurance. The Government has turned around and imposed an additional burden on those retired members of the Armed Forces.
I would like to make my comments this afternoon very brief.

Mr. Speaker, I also welcome this opportunity to take part in this hour of debate, a debate that is definitely a Johnny-come-lately, since the Bill has already reached the Senate, and the cheques will soon be delivered to our early retirees who are very anxious to get them. As usual, however, the NDP keeps arguing. That happens to be its specialty, and today it is again using up time that could otherwise be used for constructive debate and the well-being of Canadians. Of course the Liberal Party is in it as well-we hardly know which one is the Official Opposition- and it too is claiming that the Government is wrong and that it should do this and that. They would like to revert to the old system when money was spent without any concern for deficits. I suppose they would like to go back to a $38-billion dollar deficit, with acumulative deficit of $225 billion. Who cares! For them it was a matter of voting for what they wanted when they wanted to and hang the consequences. That is the kind of government we had then. That is the kind of government the voters threw out three years ago. And that is the kind of government they don't want back.
The early retirees realized that because of an erroneous interpretation by certain officials at the Employment Centres, they were misinformed. Some people took early retirement on the basis of the erroneous information, and that is why, we
corrected the situation. We did not do what the previous Government did. We're not stubborn. We listened to our fellow citizens. We understood their concerns in our ridings. Some time ago, early retirees as a whole said they were quite pleased with the Government's proposal. In fact, every newspaper in Canada reported so. They said they were quite pleased with that proposal to provide a full payment for those who had been treated unfairly before January 5 on the basis of misinformation on the part of senior officials.
Today, the NPD wants to keep up a certain fight. There is indeed a lot of contradictions in that Party. I remember a few years ago when they talked about the right to independence for Quebec, at some convention held in the Montreal area, and then a year later, they voted in favour of patriating the Constitution with the Trudeau team. A year later, it was no serious matter. They were still discussing the Constitution at the Montreal convention, and then we had the Meech Lake Agreement. On the one hand, they have told the members of the Parti Quebecois in Quebec: It is not good enough. But when they turn to English Canadians, they say: It is quite reasonable, after all, we might put up with it.
By dint of trying to flatter everybody, we will end up deceiving everybody. In this sense, not taking into account the billions of dollars which would be spent, the financial difficulties Canadians would be faced with, after investing billions of dollars in various projects, as suggested by the NDP and the Liberal Party, we would end up again with a deficit and the impossibility to improve the welfare of Canadians by concrete and precise legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate and rectify the errors which the Hon. Member for Richelieu has just made. When referring to the early retirees and pension issue, Mr. Speaker, the first thing which any Member of this House should do would be to praise the Hon. Member for Montreal

Sainte-Marie for his tremendous contribution. All Hon. Members know that it is thanks to the efforts made by the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie and the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) that 35,000 early retirees who had been so unfairly treated by this Conservative Government, were finally able to collect their benefits.
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
It is unfortunate that the Member for Richelieu (Mr. Plamandon) did not take the time to listen to the Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart), who could have briefed him very well on the subject. If he had listened, his intervention would have been far more valuable than that which we heard. I say that with respect for my hon. friend from Richelieu, for whom I have a lot of respect. However, in this particular case he appears to be very poorly informed, as I am sure you have noticed, Mr. Speaker.
We all know that these retirees were unilaterally cut off after paying into the unemployment insurance fund for years and years. That is equivalent to telling someone who had a car accident that their policy was changed last night and they will not be paid for the car accident. If you were told that, you would obviously ask what you had been paying premiums for if you are not covered, and if you are not covered, why you were not told that you would not be covered before you were asked to pay premiums. Would that not be reasonable? Surely it would.
I know that all Members of this House, and particularly you, Sir, who is nonpartisan in this debate, understand that perfectly well. I am sure that if the Tory Members across stopped and thought a little bit they would understand too.

Mr. Speaker, on December 5, 1986, the Conservative Government finally admitted it was wrong. The Government said through its Minister: I am guilty. That is what the Government said. It was guilty of having caused early retirees so much grief.
However, having admitted its guilt, the Government said: Sure, I am guilty, but I going to help you just a little bit. So, they reimbursed 35,000 early retirees who had contributed all their lives like so many others, and who had already retired when the Minister changed the legislation and took away their benefits.
Mr. Speaker, some had even resigned just two or three weeks before. Some of my constituents came to see me and who said: I resigned. I was entitled to receive benefits during the couple of weeks of my waiting period, but I lost that entitlement. What is going on? It's unfair! I told them: Yes, it's unfair, I agree. Mr. Speaker, it is unfair. That is Conservative justice, Mr. Speaker. Justice for the rich but no justice for the poor.
Through Bill C-50, the Government has reimbursed 35,000 early retirees. That is wonderful. But it doesn't solve the problem. We have dealt with just a fraction of the problem. As far as the other group is concerned, people now have to be fired twice before they are able to draw benefits. The Hon. Member from Montreal-Sainte-Marie, with his thorough knowledge of the issues, pointed this out here in the House. I am sure that all Members of this House, all early retirees and
